div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

HEARTS may be honest, but they are always or the beat. WHEN is a lover justified in calling his sweet- heart honey When she is bee-loved. WHAT sort of a room is best suited for pokei playing? Why, an ante-room, of course. "I SAY, Jim, if a fellow took sulphuric acid what would you give him 7" "I'd give him up." WHEN is a pretty girl inclined to commit murder? When she is bound on a sleighing expedi- tion. A THING of beauty is a joy forever, if you are wise enough to let some other fellow marry her. ." YES, sir," said Popinjay, emphatically, "Grab- all is a man of limited means but unlimited mean- ness." "BILLY, my boy, can't you eat a little more ?" Well, I don't know but I could, mother, if I stood up." IN Denmark most of the girls are trained in agriculture. In this country the girls take more kindly to husbandry. THERE is one kind of vice which never sticks to. young people enough to hurt them, and that is advice. A FATHER, in reproving his son, said sternly to him, "Did you ever see me doing such a thing as that when I was a boy 7" THERE is one class of men who must invariably have "their glass" before they can do their work successfully. They are glaziers. A YOUNG MAN pointed to a rich and handsome lady, who said to his friend: "Hasn't she a comely figure?" "Yes, an incomely figure," was the reply. A GERMAN BARON is said to have secured a place ES waiter in a New York restaurant. It is only natural that he should take to the fodderland. • THERE'S a man up town so cranky that he won't live in a house with trees in front of it, because, as he says, their bark disturbs him at night. IT is an old adage that "Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown. It is equally true that uneasy lies the head that wears a ,presidential bee on its crown. CHARLES LAMB said of the water-cure: "It is neither new nor wonderful, for it is as old as the Deluge, whickin my opinion, killed more than it cured." NIAGARA LANDLORD—"YOR look tired and thirsty. Won't 'yen have a' glass of water?" Cautious Visitor (who has read about the Falls)— "How much is it? " Mn. DRYGOODS—" What a lovely colour Miss Jones ,has I I declare, she looks like a chromo." Miss Smallwares—" A chrome I had the impres- sion that she was hand painted." ROBIN, who had just commenced the study of the French language, on being aektel by his father why an indiscretion was like an enemy, replied; "Because it is a faux pas" (Foe, pa.). AFTER rolling all night in your berth at sea, till you are miserably sick, it is irritating to have the steward open the door in the morning and ask if you will have a fresh roll for breakfast. "Sam, did you see Mr. Jenkins, the newoverseer ?" "Yes, massa ; I meet him down by the cotton-gin." "He's a good-looking fellow, isn't he?" "Well, massa, he talks like a good-looking man. He made a bow; dat's all he said." TOURIST (to boy fishing)—"How many fish have you caught, my man 7" Boy—" Oh, I couldn't count 'ern I" Tourist—'• Why, you haven't caught any, you little vagabond l" Boy—" That's why I can't count 'em "WHERE did you board this summer?' a gentle- man asked of a friend on his return from his vaca- tion trip. "Oh I" replied, "there was no trouble about getting bored: I got bored wherever I went." "AREN'T you tired of this vacation, ma 7" asked a bright little fellow. "I'm tired of the noise you make," the mother replied. "An' I'm awful tired of the noise you make tryin' to stop the noise I make," responded the tired urchin. • GOOD GOVERNMENT.—A mad princess of the house of Bourbon, on being asked why the reigns of- -queens were, in general, more prosperous than the reigns of kings, replied: "Because under kings women govern—under queens, men." A TEMPERANCE leciurer in New Hampshire Ilnished his discourse thus: "Finally my hearers, why should any of you drink ardent spirits? My son Tom has got as good cider as any in the country, -at six cents per quart I" A TRAVELLER in Holland asked a man whom be saw at work on the highway, "Where does this road go to?" The man looked dazed, and after rubbing his forehead, said: "I don:t know, sir. I finds it here when I comes to work in the morning, and I leaves it here at night; but where it goes when I ain't here I don't know." ON a sign, over a store in a New England village, the following was painted: "Dry Goods; by John Bagster ; Who Wishes to get Married." This sign drew all kinds of customers. The single ladies went as a matter of course, and the married men told their wives to go, under the impression that they could easily get good bargains out of such a great fool. A STRANGER riding along a road, observing that the mile stones were turned so as to face the fields, called to a farmer at work near by and inquired the reason. "Why, bless you, sir," replied the farmer, "the wind is sometimes so strong in these parts that if we (:lidn't turn the hacks of the mile-stones to it the figuies wSeild all be blown off them, clear and clean." A KNOWING HOTEL KEEPEIL—There is a hotel In Philadelphia that only charges half price for lovers, and the proprietor says he makes more money out of this class of boarder than any other people about the house. "Let a youth," he says, "sit up with a yellow spencer and blue eyes on Sunday night, and he will feel so heavenly that he won't get down to pork and beans again till the latter part of the week." LOVE AND LAW.—A young, lawyer who had long paid his court to a lady without much advancing his snit, accused her one day of "being insensible to the power of love." "It does not follow," she archly replied, "that I am so, because I am not to be won by the power of attorney." "Forgive me," replied the suitor, "but you should remember that all the votaries of Cupid are solicitors." SOMETHING LIKE A RELIC.—A traveller on the continent, visiting a celebrated cathedral, was shown by the sacristan, among other marvels, dirty opaque phial. After eyeing it some time, the traveller said: "Do you call this a relic 7" " Sir," said the sacristan, indignantly, "it contains some of the darkness that was spread over the land of EgYPt." A SHIP having sprung a leak, a green hand was set at work at the pump. Before be began pump- ing he looked over the rail to see how high the water was on the side of the vessel. After working an hour he again took a peep over the side, and finding the vessel was four inches deeper than when he began, he exclaimed: " Armh, captain, I shall soon pump the sea fullht this rate, for I have raised it four inches already!" A WELL-KNOWN New York physician says that he was once rung up in the middle of the night, and requested by a man to call immediately upon his wife. "Very well," said the doctor. "How much will it cost?" asked the caller: "Ten dollars —to go that distance to-night." "How much will It be if you call in the morning?" "Two dollars.* •• Well, call ill the morning," said the husband. • NOTE:NCI LIKE KNOWING HOW.—Some soldiers were (I.:4ging a welt in one of the forts in the West. When they came to the water the commanding officer s.ent to inspect progress. "Well, Cowan," said he to the Irishman at the bottom of the well, "you have found the water at last!" " Ah, eel," replied the other, "it all dipinds upon know- ing how the thing ought to be done. Any other man but myself would have gone forty fut deeper without corning to it !" BOBBY, a precocious youth of six summers, had been indulging in bad language, and in order to escape the, punishment for which his mother had made preparations he crawled under a barn, and , remained there in a state of siege for the greater part of an afternoon. When his father returned at night and learned how matters stood, he made his way, with much difficulty, under the barn in search of the boy. "Hallo, papa,' said Bobby, cheerfully, as his sire approached, "is mam after you? Have you been saying something wicked, too?" A LADY in a car who was greatly annoyed by the whistling of a man a few seats behind her remarked to a friend: "It is said that the whistling man is one who thinks little. But he makes others think; and, oh, what dreadful thoughts they think, tool"

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
"Mr. Hamish MacCunn is at present engaged upon a new arrangement of the songs of &offend!' What's the matter with the present arrangement? They want modeinising, perhaps.
Jacques, the Frenchman who-tried to rival Sum at the Aquarian, has begun a forty days' fast at Christiania. A glass room has been constructed for him. Succi is operating in New York.
London possesses one lady stockbroker, one lady landscape gardener, and one lady denti,t. Curiously enough, these ladies have found no imitators, though they have all been established some time.

Should the Speaker maintain his resolution to resign, it is probable that the House will appoint Mr. Courtney his deputy. Mr. Peel has been in bad health lately, and is very much depressed by the death of his wife.

News conies from Washington of a highly com- mendable innovation, which, it may be hoped, will soon become the fashion in London. The invitation cards to a "smart" wedding which recently took place there bore in the left-Ivand corner this pleas- ing intimation "No presents."

Mr. Gladstone's carriage, as he left the Princess's Theatre on Saturday evening, was surrounded, says a correspondent, by a crowd principally composed of Irishmen who cheered him lustily. One enthu- siastic young man going to the window cried out, "Ireland is with you, Mr. Gladstone; never mind Parnell." At this the cheers were vigorously re- newed.

It is a somewhat singular ,coincidence that Car- dinal -Newman, Dr. Liddon. and the Dean of St. Paul's bhoulcl have ,died nvtihin a few months of each other. Cardinal Newviran and Dr. Church were intimate friends, and Dr. Liddon and the late dean were kindred spirits. Dr. Church has held the deanery of St. Vaal's since 1871, having been appointed by Mr.,Gladstoue on the death of Dean Milman.

A correspondent writes :—" I think you are mis- taken in doubting that Sir Robert Peel once con- templated challenging Mr. Disraeli. The "distin- guished friend" was the Duke of Newcastle. Sir Robert was so cut to the quick at Dizzy's attacks on him that he asked the Duke to take a message, and the Duke had great difficulty in calming him down. I heard this story from several people just as Froud relates it, and I was not his informant.

Tit-bit from the " World":—" Lord Mortis gets. credit, whether rightly or not I cannot say, for the mot, which is so popular at this moment, that it is but right that Mr. Parnell should retire and enjoy his O'Shea (m) sum dignitate. (Mr. Plunkett is also credited with the authorship, of that estimable jest.) Equally humorous is the remark of a well- known cynical M.P. to the effect that it was now time all the adulterers should stand shoulder to shoulder."

Lord Houghton was one of the most agreeable ot men, but be had one defect. He wore false teeth, and they were always falling about in a strange manner. The following story was told of him. He was in a railway carriage. A lady got in, and sat down opposite him. In a second she jumped up, "Some one is biting me," she shrieked. And it turned out that Lord Houghton had pat his teeth on the seat, and that they closed on her when she sat down.

The following anecdote of 'a minor light of the Irish Bench, thought not precisely a " bull " pure and simple, belongs more or less to that fertile family. A wife had suffered unto • hands of a barbarous ,an in self-defence she "took the Ira ;" but just before the trial shazelau ,and told the judge she wished to leave the punishment and the case to God. " I regret my good woman," replied the great official.; "that we cannot do that; the case is far too important."

Without 'pretending to rival Dr. Koch or M. Pasteur, Mr. Justice Hawkins has established a fair claim to a place among the discoverers of cures. At the Chelmsford Assizes last week a prosecutor had begun to give his evidence in half-inaudible tones, when this judge, with that twinkle in the eye which is sofamiliar to gentlemen at the bar, ob- served " 1 will giv'b you something for your throat. Remember that 1 shall not allow you any expenses if you don't speak louder." The prescription is stated to have been at once attended by "a mar- vellous cure."

An extraordinary state of things has developed itself in connection with the business of scale and weighing machine manufacturers. On the Ist of January a new Act comes into operation requiring the special stamping of all machines in use on that dayi. The manufacturers find themselves quite un- able to grapple with the orders crowding in upon trern, and an effort is being made to induce the President of the Board of Trade to grant an exten- sion of time for fixing the Government stamp. Mr. Causton is in communication on the subject with Sir M. Hicks-Beach.

The inquest just concluded at Newcastle-under- Lyme should serve as a warning to Guardians. It is clear enough that the deaths of the six old women who lost their lives in the fire at the New- castle Workhouse were due entirely to the deficiency of the water supply, and equally clear that the de- ficiency in the water supply was due entirely to the negligence of the Guardians. They may think themselves lucky to have got off without a verdict of manslaughter. But hove many workhouses are there where the same state of thiasgs would be found it a fire broke out to-night?

Mr. Rudolf Lehmann, who, with Sir F. Leighton and other experts in art, gave evidence in the curi- ous case Sternberg v. Thaddeus, is the brother of Mr. F. Lehmann, of Berkeley-square, who ispartner in the house of Naylor. Benzon, and Co.. and uncle by marriage to Mr. Ernest Benson. .the Jubilee Plunger. Mr. Rudolf Lehmann is a painter of con- siderable eminence, and is particularly happy in his portraits. In his brother's dining-room in Berkeley- square, among many gems of art, hangs a most in- teresting portrait of Bobert Browning, painted some years ago by Mr. Rudolf Lehmann, who was an intimate friend of the great poet. The Lehmanns are IA talented family. Mr. F. Lehmann's eldest son, Mr. R. C. Lehmann, the rowing man, is a constant contributor to "Punch," while his niece Miss Liza Lehmann is a charming singer, well-known in Lon- don concert rooms.

The British Museum has becomq possE ssed of three Chaldean monuments which were found in litughtrider-st. (not a stone's throw from St. Paul's Cathedral) during the recent demolition of some old houses. These are supposed to have been brought over in the early part of the seventeenth century by a Dutch merchant who was known to have lived on the spot where thpy were discovered and who traded with the East Indies and ports of the Persian Gulf. The stones, through their great weight, must have fallen through the ruins of the house, at the time of the "Great Fire" of 1666, and were evi- dently unnoticed when the houses were rebuilt, they being discovered some distance below the pre- sent foundation. The monuments are of the pre- Semitic age of Ur, Nina, and Guilea, when the kccadean language was alone in use, and characters - r employed in writing were of the most archaic form.

The death of M. William Gregson, at Blackburn, will cause widespread regret in the temperance world. He was born at Ribchester on the 2nd of , March, 1820, where is father, a gardener, was parish clerk. Mr. Gregson began life as a hano-loom lweaver, but in 1834 the younger part of the family migrated to Clitheroe, and became power-loom weavers. It was whilst the factory hand at the Low Moor Mill that he became interested in the temperance movement. In 1849 he was appointed teetotal missionary at Blackburn at a salary of 15s. per week, and he refused to cancel the engagement when a position at more than double the "salary " was offered to him. In the pursuance of his'teeto- tal propaganda, it is said that he visited every town and village in the land Vora John O'Groat's to Land's End. In the earlier days such orators were not infrequently greeted with rotten eggs and other missiles from the mob, whilst the police were almost equally apt to bring them before the magis- trates for the obstruction of .thorouglifares. In these legal encounters Mr. Gregson's astuteness usually brought him off victor. Gregson was a good friend to popr Critchley Prince, whose fine talents were Man. ed by habitual intemperance. To him the post inscribed his " Angel of Temperance," written during one of his efforts to escape from drunkenness.

div.head: WORKS ON THE
div.p: WORKS ON THE
SPRINCH, RUNCORN.
CHANGES BY THE SHIP CANAL.

Amongst the changes brought about in the Run- corn district by the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, the most important is that of the efface- ment of what is locally known as the Old Quay Yard, the headquarters of the engineering depart- ment of the Bridgewater Navigation Company.. There was every appliance at the Old Quay for the building and repainng of the numerous craft of that firm, and being also the terminus of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, there were cJnamodious docks for dealing with the traffic of that not unim- portant waterway, which was the property of the Bridgewater Company. In order to carry out their vast scheme, the directors of the Ship Canal Com- pany had to acquire the two canals, at an enormous outlay of money, and Old Quay Yard and Old Quay Docks are to disappear. And of necessity, because between Warrington and Runcorn, the Ship Canal crosses the Runcorn and Latchford Canal no less than tour times, and cuts through the centre ot Old Quay Docks as it eaters the Mersey. The Mersey and Irwell have existed as a navigable channel from Manchester to Warrington since 1720, but the capitalists who spent their money in making the ' navigation, lost by their enterprise, and in 1780 it was disposed of to the 'Mersey and Irwell Navigation, who, in 1803, in order to navigate during neap tides in their trade with Liverpool, extended the navigation to Run- corn, this portion being known as the Runcorn and Latchford Canal. This extension cost £48,000. In 1828 commodious docks and improved locks were constructed at Runcorn at a further cost of £60,000. Some years later the property was acquired by the Bridgewater Trustees, and subsequently by the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company, as stated, and now has to disappear alto- gether before the steam diggers of the new waterway. But engineering sheds and boat building yards are still a necessity for the Bridgewater Undertaking, which is, being carried on as successfully as ever, otherwise a sad loss would have befallen the town, as 200 skilled work- men are employed in the work. New works have been erected on the Sprinch, a suitable locality on the banks of the Btidgewater Canal, and the migration from the old to the new is now taking place. As most of our readers are perhaps not aware the Sprinch is an island. When Brindley made the Bridgewater Canal he had to go in a loop at that point in order to get solid ground to work upon. Ii that far off day the Sprinch was a wooded ravine 40 feet deep, through the bottom of which flowed a stream of clear water. Since then tlse ravine has been filled with chemical and other refuse of various kinds from the neighbouring works ; and, as the traffic at this point is very heavy, and the inconvenience to steamers and flats in navigating the curve was a source of trouble and annoyance, it was contemplated for many years to make a straight cutting and utilize the loop for other purposes than navigation. When the Ship Canal Company took over the undertaking-the present directors at once determined to carry out the long contemplated improvement, and Mr. F. Wiswall the resident engineer, whom IW- _
d

am"dley, was entrusted Virtrare task. The material through which the new cutting had to be made, being formed of alkali waste, &c., was of a very treacherous description, and very great care and skill had to be exercised in carrying out the work, but it was happily brought to a successful conclusion without mishap of any kind. The sides of this portion of the waterway are made of concrete, and are made more secure and efficient by a double lino of puddling. This alteration makes a difference of five minutes to a tug drawing barges, in consequence of the shortening of the distance, and escaping the awkward- ness of the old curve.

It is because of this cutting that the Sprinch has been converted into an island, where the new repairing yard has beenformed, and where very large and commodious workshops have been erected in accordance with the designs of that highly respected and accomplished towns- man, Mr. Wiswall. The whole of the buildings are sub- stantially constructed in brick, on the most approved principle, with the most modern arrangement and im- provements; and the accommodation provided is much superior to that of the old works. Every comfort and facility is afforJed to the workmen in carrying on their work: The dimensions of the various places are as fol- lows :—Fitters' shop 60ft. by 50ft.; wheelwrights' shop. 40ft. by 50ft. : joiners' shop, 401 t. by 50ft. ; sawmill and pattern makers' shop, 70ft. by 50ft. All these workshops are in one block, and are supplied with a powerful engine and boiler. Close by there is a forge and boiler shed 90ft. by 150 ft. wide, and on the edge of the canal is a capital boat builder' shed. There is also an iron store, 50ft. by 40ft.

Not the least important part of the establishment are the graving dooks, which have been formed on the site of the old loop of thd canal. There are two single grav- ing docks 100 feet long by 30 feet wide, and two double graving docks 100 feet long and over 50 feet wide. They are very solidly built of bricks, faced with red sand- stone, the flooring in each instance being formed of con- crete of which a very large amount was required. These docks, although more costly' in the first instance, are much more convenient, and afford a more ready means of repairing craft, than the ordinary slipways which were in use at the old yard. Underneath these docks is a large sewer for the drainage of that part of the town, and as the water from the docks is emptied into it, the sewer will at all times be exceedingly well flushed, and those nuisances commonly arising from the sediment of sewers will be obviated.

Being situated an island, some means of communicat- ing with the "outer world" was necessary, and a Via- duct has been erected across the docks to Heath-road. The Viaduct is built of brick, in semi-circular form and consists or three arches, each having a span of 22 feet. The gradient is a very gentle one under the circum- stances, and horses with their heavy loads will have no difficulty in surrnounting the structure. Adjoining this Viaduct and facing Heath-road, admir- ably arranged offices are in course of construction, and in the same neighbourhcod a lesidence for the engineer is to be erected..

" Almost at the same spot, there is another important and difficult undertaking being carried.out by the Com- pany, and although it is not the outcome of these changes, yet there is a connection which renders it not inappro- priate to mention ia this article. That is the building of a bridge across the Big Pool,,in order to connect the pro- posed new Victoria-road with Mill Brow an Halton-road districts. The Pool will be crossed by a sffostantial and well proportioned Viaduct of no less than six arches, and again is Mr. Wiswall the designer of the plans,which will be executed under his superintendence. The Company are building this structure mainly at their own cost,and, while it will be of considerable benefit in conducting their own business, they are conferring a boon on the public, which ought ;to be gratefully remembered in the future.

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER NEAR CARDIFF.
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER NEAR CARDIFF.

Late on Monday nfght a-woman named Martha Davis,- aged 27 years, daughter of John Davies, engine-driver, of Bryander, near Cardiff, was found dead in her father's house under suspicious circumstances. The father left home for work about five o'clock on Monday evening his daughter and her two-year-old illegitimate child in the house. Shortly after eight p.m. her brother called, and found her in excellent health and spirits. Later in the evening a neighbour found her lying on her back dead in the kichen, having apparently been murderously as- saulted and outraged.

div.head: CHRISTMAS AND OTHER BOOKS.
div.p: CHRISTMAS AND OTHER BOOKS.

_ "Lady Mauda's Mania-ra tragedy in high hfe ",is the title of the' latest novel from that versatile author Mr. -George Manville Fenn. This story is altogether different from the majority of Mr. Fenn's novels which are forthe most part full of exciting adventures. Not that there is any lack of incident in the present case, but the incident, though suffi- ciently lively, i% not of a sensational character. ,Lady MAUde is the, daughter of the Earl of Bar- mouth, and is doomed by a strong-minded match- making mamma to marry- for money rather than love. Whether the mother of the maiden has her way it must be left for the story to tell. The old Earl is ,an eccentric character with sundry amiable weaknesses which keep up the high-life comedy. The son is a jolly, plucky little fellow, and Maude's lover is, of course, all that a true lover should be. The story is racily written; there is not a dull page in the book ; and the various characters are vigour- onsly drawn. " Maude's Mania" is quite out of the common run'ornovels, and'is tare to be in demand by a large body of readers. It is published by Messrs F. Warne and Co., London. The same firm have also issued the third series of" The E`ncore Reciter" ; which is edited by Mr. F. E. Marshall Steele. The selections are of a very varied kind, humorous, serious, and dramatic. They are from the best authors, and, as they include many copyright pieces, it is a matter of course to say the purchaser gets special value for his shilling investment. " Lost in Samoa" is tale of adventure in the Navigation Islands, written by Mr. E. S. Ellis, author of "Boy Pioneer Series," &c., and it is printed and published by Messrs. Cassell and Co. The tale is well told, and steadily increases in interest until an exciting climax is reached. It presents a vivid picture of life in Samoa, and especially of those reckless vagrants who are known as Beach Combers. The story is adorned with eight original illustrations by Mr. Gordon Brown, who, it should be said, has thoroughly realized what the author describes. "Perils Afloat and Brigands Ashore," by Mr. Alfred Elwes, author of" Paul Blake,"" Swift and Sure," &c., is another volume of the class last noticed, published by 'Messrs. Cassell and Co. As the title would suggest, the story abounds in adventure both by land and sea, and the writer is to be credited with the natural way in which he brings every strange thing to pass. This story is also capitally illustrated by Mr. Gordon Brown; and, it should be added that alike Lost in Scamp.; while it is calculated to interest all classes, it is es- pecially adapted to delight youthful readers. Either work would be treasured as a Christmas gift to. the young. " Ravenswoods "is the title of a shilling sovenir of the play as presented at the Lyceum Theatre by Mr. Henry Irvin.. It is illustrated in a really admirable way by Mr. J. B. Partridge, J. Barker, and H. Craven. There is no mistaking the likeness in the principal characters, but what pleases one more is the effective way in whim the finest scenes are reproduced. This souvenir is, in its way, a work of art of no mean order. "Yule Tide," as a Christmas number, is in no respect behind its predecessors, which is about the best criticism that can be passed upon it. "I saw three ships," by the author of" Dead man's rock," is the title of an ad- mirable story which runs through the number. The principal coloured picture is the reproduction of the painting by W. Joy, entitled "Prince Charley's farewell to Laura &acdonafe," and there are, besides, four full- plate/pictures namely, " Sweet seventeen," " Sweeter seventy," "Drawing together," and "Our yule tide invaders." They are all highly finished works and in every way a credit to Messrs. Cassell. " Holly Leaves," is the Christmas number of the "Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic Gazette." It is accompanied with two coloured plates as supplements, "Fancy free," by R. Madrazo, and "The cats' Christ- mas dance," by L. Wane, who, in his characteristic way satirises human nature in this comical illustration of a feline Christmas party. The number is in other respects amply illustrated, and there is a large variety of Christ- mas reading. . _ .

newspaper, and Court Chronicle," has for its presenta- tion plate, a powerful reproduction of the picture by Van Der Bos, known as "Queen and Heir,' besides a smaller plate of "The eve of St. Nicholas," being a Watteau study by E. Griviz. Both are excellent, and the latter, especially, is a dainty specimen of chromolitho- graphy. The frontispiece of the number is adorned with portraits of the Queen, and the Empresses of Austria, Germany and Russia. The illustrations of English women and children are excellent, and the same must be said of the children's fancy dresses, suggestions for artis- tic work, glimpses of Geneva, and other places on the continent, by the Duchess of Rutland. "The Century Magazine," for December has for the frontispiece a beautifully-finished head of "Daphne," fawn the painting by Mr ft. W. Maynard. The first illustrated article is on "Life in California before the gold discovery ;" and the other illustrated articles are "Franklin in Allegory" (with a portrait of Benjamin Franklin) ; "Laurels of the American tar in 1812;" "the cynical Miss Catherwaight ; " "Col. Carter, of Cartersville ;" "the border land of China," /to., con- eluding with bric-a-brac, which is alike clever in text an, l illustration. _

"The English Illustrated Magazine," is, as usual for December, published as a double number, the price being one shilling. The frontispiece is a fine portrait of George Vyashington, engraved by 0. Lacour, and following on there is an illustrated paper on the ancestral home of the Washingtons. "A Painter of Players," by J. F. Mulloy, is admirably illustrated, and the same criticism applies to "Inns and taverns of old London," by Phillip Nor- man. The Rey. Doctor H. Kingston contributes "The Frogmousaid," which is characteristically, that is to say, cleverly illustrated by Lewis Wane, "Nooks and corners of Westminster Abbey," by the Venerable and A.rchdeacon Farrar, is illustrated by Mr. Herbert„Railton in style which shows that his hand has not lost its cunn- ing, but rather increased it. There are other papers and stories which add to the impression that the England Illustrated makes a hit as heretofore with its Christmas number.

" Scribuer's Magazine" has a cover of chocolate and gold in token of its being a Christmas number. The lead- ing paper is one by Sir Edwin Arnold, with illustrations by Mr. Robert Blurnm, and its title is "Japonica," by which is meant some account of Japan, where Sir Edwin now resides. The illustrations, it should be stated, are powerful pieces of work, the artist t.eing a master in his capacity to suggest colour by means of black and white. 6. A pastoral, without words," tells its tale in a very pretty style. Other illustrated papers, &c., include 6. Amy, Robsert, Kennilworth, and Warwick "; " Christie's ";" My disreputable friend, Mr. Raegan ; and " Neopolitan Art—Morelli." The stories and verse maintain the high average of the magazine which con- cludes, as usual, with "The point of view." Newbury House Magazine," for December leads off with Christmas and other amusement at the East end by the Bishop of Bedford, followed by Christmas in art and legend; the church and national thrift ; Triolese Christ- mas customs; a man's notes in a nursery ; a Christmas school treat in Bengal, &c. Several stories are illustrated; and, as the magazine concludes with a Christmas story for children, it will be recognised that the current issue is au out and out seasonable number.

div.head: AN AUSTRALIAN'S PA ItLIAMENTARy
div.p: AN AUSTRALIAN'S PA ItLIAMENTARy
EXPERIENCE.

The "Star" says :—Here is how a visiting Australian who was lately with us has been narrating his experi- ences with unaffected candour and delightful naivete : "I have been to the House of Commons several times, and listened to some good debates. John Morley is the best speaker I have heard, except, perhaps, Gladstone. I was very anxious to hear a debate in the House of Lords. I found some difficulty in getting an order, so I determined to follow the popular advice, and 'ask a ple'ceman.' I went to the policeman on duty, and re- quested him to tell me when he saw a lord passing. The bobby entered into the Jun of the thing, and quickly pointed out the desired object. I went up anti greeted the nobleinan,telling him that I was from Australia, and that I had a great desire to get inside the House of Lords. He shook me warmly by the hand, apologised for having to leave me for a few minutes in order to procure the pass, returned almost iMmediately, took me in, and re- mained with me some ten or fifteen minutes pointing out all the leading men in the House. He then bade me I an affectionate good-bye, and said that he envied me liv- ing in Australia. Who do you think that the noble lord I was? The Earl of Aberdeen. He is a thorough man, and has evidently not forgotten the welcome that he re- ceived in Australia. I heard Salisbury and Granville speak—as speakers they are equal to any men in the I other House."

div.head: LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS.
div.p: LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS.
BY L. GORDON RYLANDS, B.A. (Concluded.)

It will be said that Mr. Rylands was not com- pelled thus to sacrifice his principles, that a mem- ber of Parliament is not a delegate, .and that it was his duty to act according to his convictions whether his constituents liked it or not. This is quite true, and I have not one word .to say in defence of the course Mr. Rylands then took, but I may plead cer- tain things in extenuation. Mr. Rylands was get- ting on in years, and to be obliged to find and work up a new constituency would have been very irk- ' some to him, more especially as failing health, the result largely of over-work, rendered him disin- clined for much. exertion; under these circum- stances the loss of his seat at Burnley would have been practically equivalent to the termination of his public career. Burnley suited him, he liked the Burnley people and they liked him. What wonder then if he hesitated to take a step which might alienate the good will of his strongest supporters in that borough ? Besides, if the Government had , been turned out lie did not believe that any other could have been formed in which he could have confidence. I might also plead that it is of almost daily occurrence for members of Parliament to sacrifice their principles for party or personal ends, but if a man has done wrong it would be no extuse for him could he say that everyone else has done wrong too, though it might be to some extent a palliation of his conduct. In the very case of which we are speaking other Liberal members actqd in the same way, some of thein even members of the Government. Mr. Chamberlain repeatedly expressed to Mr. Rylands his disapproval of the Coercion Bill, telling him that Mr. John Bright was equally opposed to it, and urged him to vote against the Bill. Mr. Rylands replied, "No; if I, and other Radicals oppose this Bill, our constituents will say to us that if Bright and Chamberlain, whose Liberalism is be- yond question, can support Mr. Gladstone on this ques- tion, surely they may expect us to do so. No ! we won't sacrifice ourselves, but if you and Bright will resign we will not hesitate to support you." 'However, Mr. Chamberlain would not resign, for though he would have been pleased enough to see Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment overthrown by the votes of others, he was not the man to burn his fingers in pulling the chestnuts out of the fire for himself. Another measure of the Government which Mr. Rylands regarded with intense dislike was the adoption of the Cloture, and in this case again he refrained from opposing the Government, in conformity with the wishes of his constituents.
The conduct of the Irish members also made Parlia-

mentary life less pleasant than it 11.a:cf.-Previously been, the all-night sittings; and the occasional strong language indulged in by some members of the Irish party, to- gether with their general obstructive tactics, gradually rendered that party distasteful to him, and having once become prejudiced against them he began to credit the many current reports as to their complicity with crime in Ireland. This dislike was much intensified by the action of the Irish party with regard to the elections in 1885, and he was extremely annoyed that Mr. Parnell should request the Irish voters in Burnley to oppose him, as he considered that he was entitled to the gratitude of the Irish people, quite forgetting that in their estimation all obligations had been cancelled by the Coercion Act. In the year 1885, therefore, Mr. Rvlands was domi- nated by two powerful feelings : a feeling of distrust and dislike of Mr. Gladstone, which had grown, little by little, since 1880, until it amounted almost to a mono- mama ; and a feeling 01 disgust at the Irish party. Half- a-dozen years previous to this he would never have allowed his judgment to be warped, by prejudices such as ihese, but overwork during the sessions 1868-74, 1874-80 had worn out his constitution. His health was now very'seriously impaired—far more so than he him- self or any of his friends ever suspected, and in conse- quence of this failing of bodily vigour, there was bound to be a failing of intellectual vigour his mind was no

could no longer view a question under all its different aspects, and take the same broad view of acts and events; a feeling of weariness and disinclination for change had cc me over him. I myself heard hita remark about this time that" really, there is very little differ- ence now between Liberals and Conservatives: so much has been done in the last years, such rapid progress has been made, that there is scarcely anything which urgently calls for reform." It will now be easy for anyone to understand the atti- tude which Mr. Rylands adopted in relation to Mr. Glad- stone's Home Rule Bill. In fact, there was nothing at all surprising about it. Supposing that any one be- forehand had been asked to consider this hypothetical case : on the one hand, a man who intensely disliked and distrusted Mr. Gladstone, who was extremely an- noyed at the conduct of the Irish members, and who even believed them capable of countenancing crime, and who had begun to long for intellectual rest, and view with disquietude any political change ; on the other hand, a measure proposed by Mr. Gladstone to satisfy the demands of those frish members, and supported by them, and embodying a political change of such magni- tude as to be almost revolutionary. Now put the ques- tion, what will he the attitude of that man towards that measure? There is but one answer possible,—he will certainly oppose-it„,, Mr. Rylands' opPbsition to Home Rule probably caused more astpnishment, especially among Liberals, than thel opposition of any other man. The majority of the dis- sentient* were Whigs. Everyone knew that they were only waiting for such an opportunity of seceding te the Conservative party. In the case of other Radicals it was not difficult to suspect interested motives. But Mr. Ry- lands was regarded as an advanced Radical, and he was known to be a man whose honesty was beyond question. The news of his defection therefore, came upon Burnley Liberals, and, indeed, Liberals all over the country, as a great shock. They did not know that failing health and increasing age had made him more a Conservative than a Radicarm his sympathies; and they did not know that, owing to the decay of mental vigour, he had al- lowed two powerful prejudices so to obscure his judg- ment as to prevent him forming an impartial opinion on any matter upon which they were able to operate. Had he been ten years younger he would have taken a diffe- rent course ; and his numerous admirers, who viewed with grief a line of action so opposed to his earlier con- victions, and so different from his former actions, un- derstanding how he came to follow such a line, would banish from their minds all desire to blame, even if they entertained any, which they do not; for it is certain that those thousands of men who have been fired by his earnest words, and who have admired his integrity and honesty of purpose, remember only the great -measures of progress which he helped to pass and the many years o self-sacrificing devoted to the public ser- vice,li toil which he ich he wore himself away. a toil u w It may be that if Mr. Rylands had retired from public life in 1885 his health might have been restored. It is impossible to say, but certainly he was quite unfit to go through such a trying ordeal as the election of 1886. To find the bulk of his former supporters in opposition to him ; to see that many of those who were formerly his most aident admirers condemned him ; to be accused, in the heat of a bitter controversy, of having been actu- ated by unworthy motives; to be obli..ved to fight for victory as, perhaps, he had never fought since the first Warrington election, if even then—such physical and mental trials as these might have broken down the health of a strong man, how much more, then, that of one ,whose constitution was already seriously, under- mined? It is not too mulch to Atty that, this election hastened his death. He gained a narrow victory, hardly earned, but was not allowed to enjoy it, for very serious symptoms shortly after appeared, and, in spite of all that doctors could do, he slowly but steadily sank, and eventually expired, unconscious and free from pain, early in the morning of Tuesday, February the 4th, 1887. His death was a loss to politics, for public men of his stamp are not too common. He was a thoroughly able, Conscientious, and hard-working man. Be honestly strove to do his duty, and at the close of his life could have truly declared that his exertions had assisted in making the world a little better when he left it than it was when he entered it. Well would it be if every man could say the same.
CHARGE OF CRUELTY AGAINST A WARRINGTON FARMFR. A JUDICIAL SEPARATION GRANTED.

In the Divorce Division on Monday, before Mr. Justice Butt, Mrs. Elizabeth Warburton, proprie- tress of a farm at Burtonwood, sued for a judicial separation on the ground of her husband's cruelty. Mr. B. A. Pritchard (instructed by Messrs, Jenkins and Unsworth, of Warrington), appeared for the petitioner, and Mr. Searle (insrtucted by Messrs. War- ing, Cropper, and Co., of Liverpool), for the respondent. Petitioner was married to the respondent, John Warbur- ton, who was a farmer, at Chester, on the 7th March, 1887. and there had been ten children of the marriage. In 1889 the petitioner took a farm at Burtonwood. She alleged that on various occasions her husband had been guilty of acts of violence towards her. On one occasion she Said he pointed a min at her, and on another occa- sion jammed her arm.'between a door. The respondent I went i kto the box and denied the cruelty. The Judge referred to contradictory statements made by him in his letters and in the evidence he was giving, and stopped his counsel, asking if he thought it necessary to go fur- ther with the case, as he should not believe another word the responnent said. Mr. Searle having asked a few more questions, the Judge said : This is a very bad c..se. As I have said, I don't believe the respondent. I grant a decree of judicial separation, with costs.— Addressing the petitioner's counsel, the Judge said: What do you want with regard to the children ?—Mr. Pritchard : We want the custody of the eight,younger children.—The Judge : You shall have it. div.head: GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
div.p: THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANIIS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER VIII.

THE MASK FALLS FROM THE VILLIAN'S FACE. It was about two weeks after the event last re- corded that Rosalind Valdai sat in her own apart- ment with Zenobie for her companion. It was in the afterAoon. and a severe storm was raging with- out. _

• Now, Zenobie," spoke the beautiful maiden, "we have a moment alone—the first since morning. And now tell me about that black monk. What did he say his name was ? " " Valdimir." " Ah, yes. I have heard his name; and if I mis- take not he is a sort of mysterious being." "us is, my mistress l and I am just as confident that I have seen him before as I am that I have seen you before." " How ? Seen him before ? "
Yes." I,'BEtt where?"

" Ah," returned the young girl, with a dubious shake of the head, "there is a mystery. Por the life of me I cannot tell. He kgew me—he knows everybody—and yet he has not been long in the city, if one might judge from his conversation." "6 But what did he atop you for? Where was it?" asked Rosalind, eagerly. "It was in the church he stopped me—in our church of St. Stephen. He was at the altar, and he beckoned to me as I rose to come out. I went to him, and he asked about you." "About me ? " ")es—and about Runic Nevel." "And what about us ? " the maiden asked blush- ing._ _

Ile asked me if I thought you loved the young gun-maker. He was so kind—and he appealed so anxious to know—and then he seemed to take such an interest .in Ruric that I could not refuse to answer him."

" But what did you tell him ?" "I told him you did love Ruric. I told him how you had been children together and how you mould now give your hand to him sooner than to the proudest noble in the hand. He asked me some things about the duke, but I would not tell him that. When I must tell of evil if I tell the truth, I will not speak if I can properly avoid it." "You were right, Zenobie. You were very right —about this last part ; but you should not have told all you knew concerning Runic and me." - " I hope I did nothing wrong. Oh, I should be proud to acknowledge my love for such a man." "Aye—and so I am, my little sprite. I love Runic with my whole soul, and would be proud to give him my hand this day; but that is no reason why you should tell of it." Surely, my mistress, I meant no harm," the young girl cried, eagerly. "Hush, Zenobie. Ido not blame you, Only I would have you careful." "And I Would be careful. But oh, you could not have resisted him.' He drew iefrom me almost ere _ _ .

I knew it. He put his questions in such a strange manner that I could.not speak without telling what he wanted to know. He did not say, • Does she ye Runic Nevel ?' but he took it for granted that s ich was the case, and then ere I was aware of it he had made me say so. But he surely does not mean you harm ; nor does he mean harm to Run i Rune. He s a good man, I know." "I wish I could see him," returned Rosalind, half to herself. not mistake him if you ever do see him,
retage:4ooking m of n•

my migfresv:---krer ; an. then he dresses differently from most Of our church officers. He dresses all in black—to-day he was in black velvet But his shape is most striking charac- teristic. He is ebe fattest man in Moscow. His belly shakes when he laughs, and his chin seems to sink clear out of sight. He would be a funny man, and would make me laugh, if he did not puzzle me so.': "And did he ask you about anything else?" "No—only he asked me if I knew how the duke stood with the emperor; and I told him I thought he stood very well. Then he said he had heard that they had had some dispute concerning the duel between the Count Datnanoff and Ruric. But I told him I guessed that had resulted in no estrangement. for the duke was as much at court as ever. And after that he told me about the duel, as he was there and saw nearly the whole of the affair." And Zenobie went on and told all that the monk related about Rune's bravery; and Rosalind listened now attentively and eagerly. It was a theme that pleased her. The attendant saw how gratefully the account came upon the ears of her mistress, and she closed the recital with some opinions of her own wherein Ruric Nevel was held up as a pattern after which all men who wished to win the love of woman should be made.

But before any answer could be made by Rosa- lind the door of the apartment was opened and the duke entered. He smiled very kindly as he bowed to his ward, and then, with a wave of his hand, he motioned for Zenobie to withdraw; and after the attendant was gone he took a seat close by his fair charge. The maiden looked up into his face, and though there was no very literious look there as yet, still she could plainly see that he had something of more than usual importance on his mind. She shuddered as slies*gazed upon him, for she could not help it. There was something in the look of the man—a sort of hidden intent which came out in his tone and glance—a deep meaning, something which he had never spoken, but which was yet manifest, that moved her thus. What it was she could not tell. It was the prompting of that instinct of the human soul which may repel an object while yet the working mind detects no harm. But she was not to remain in the dark much , longer. The Evil One was loose/and his bonds of restraint were cast off. lie had marked his prey, and the mashes were gathering about it. "Rosa- lind," the duke said, in a tone which he meant should have been easy and frank, but which, never- theless, was marked strongly with effort, " there is some talk among the surgeons now that Conrad Damonoff may recover." " Oh, I am glad of that," the fair girl uttered earnestly. " Yes—l suppose so," resumed Olga, eyeing her sharply. " But you have no particular care for him, I presume." . .

A For—for—the count ? " " Aye—it was of him I was speaking." "No sir. I only care for him as I care for all who need to become better ere they die." " Aha—yes," said the duke biting his lip, for in his own mind he had the frankness to acknowledge that he was about as needy of virtue as was the count. " But," he resumed, with a faint smile, "you never loved the man ? " "No, sir," the maiden answered, gazing up into her guardian's face with an inquisitive look. "So I thought—so I thought." As Olga thus spoke he smiled again, and moved his chair nearer to Rosalind. "r am well aware," he resumed, "that youraffections have not yet been set upon any one who is capable of making a proper com- panion for you through all the ups and downs of life."

Rosalind's eyes dropped beneath the steady gaze of the speriker, and her frame trembled. But ere she could make any reply the duke went on : "My dear Rosalind, I have come now upon a business which I may justly call the most important of my life. I have not approached this subject lightly, nor with over zeal; but I have come to it through careful consideration and anxious study." Here the Duke stopped and gazed into Rosa- lind' s face. She met his gaze, and her eyes drooped again. She trembled more than before, and a dim, dreadful fear worked its way to her mind. "Rosalind," the nobleman continued, " when I was but nineteen years of age I was married with a girl whom I loved. She lived with me four short, happy years. In that time we were blessed with two children, but they lived not long to cheer us. And then my beautiful wife died, and the world was all dark and drear to me. I thought I should never love again. ,Time passed on, and you were placed in my charge. When you first came I loved you ; and I wondered if you were to take llie place of the children I had lost. But you grew quickly up. Your mind was expanded, and your heart was large. I found that I could not make a add of you; and then I sat down all alone and asked myself what place it was you had assumed in ny heart. Can you guess the answer, Rosalind ?" " As a little child," answered the maiden trem- bling violently. "No, no, sweet one. I pondered and I studied; and I examined myself carefully; and I found that the memory of my departed wife was fast fading away before the rising of another one just as pure and just as holy. Now do you understtnd ?" " No, no—oh, no !" the maiden uttered in a frightened whisper. Then listen further," continued thE nobleman

in a low, earnest tone, and with a strange fire in his. deep blue eye: "As your charms of both mind and person were gradually developed I came to look upon you with new feelings, or, I should say, -with the old feeling more fully developed. I looked around me'. I saw my sUmptuous palace without a legitimate female head. In my parties, I had no companion to assist and guide, and in my lone- liness I had no mate to cheer and enliven cue. I wished not that such should be the case. At, length my eyes were opened, and I plainly saw the- spirit that was moving upon my soul. I looked upon you, and I knew that I had found the woman who was to give me joy once More. Rosalind, I love you truly, fondly; and I would make you my wife. Now you cannot fail to understand me—can you?"-
Rosalind gazed up in the face of her guardian and she was as pale as death. "You do not mean—oh !"

It was a deep, painful groan, and the fair girl clasped her hands towards the man before her. "Hold," he said, almost • sternly. "I am not trifling now. I all not only serious, but firm in purpose. When you were placed under my charge your father bade me do as I would; and now I would make you my wife. The Count Damon off- was the first who came for your hand, and had be been a proper man, and had you loved him, I should have interposed no objections; but you did not love him, and the affair is past. Now I lay my claim upon you, and my fortune and title I lay at • your feet.'

And what is to become of my estate?" the maiden asked, quickly and meaningly, for the thought flashed'upon her. "Why—we'll have the two united," returned the duke, with some hesitation. "No, no," Rosalind cried; "you will not do this. Oh, spare me from such a fate I" "Spare thee, girl? Spare thee from becoming the wife of one of the most powerful noblemen in the empire? You must be crazy." "My guardian," spoke the fair girl, now looking her companion steadily in the face, •` you only do, this to try me. When you know that such a union would make me miserable forever—when youknow it would cast out all the joys of life, and extinguish the last hope of peace from my soul, you snrely will not press it." "Rosalind Valdai, I have resolved that you should. be my wife. Mind you, this is one of the firm, fixed purposes of my soul; and those who know the Duke of Tula best know that he never gives up a purpose once fixed in his mind. Yu cannot mistake me now."

Slowly the stern fact dawned upon Rosalind's mind. There had been a lingering hope that he might be only trying her to see if she loved him, or if she would willingly become his wife. Awhile she remained with her head bowed, and her bosom heav- ing with the wild emotion thus called up; but at length she looked up and spoke. "Sir," she said, faintly, but with marked decision, "you can not make me your wife." "Ah ?—and why not?" "Because I will never consent." " Ab —say ye so?" "I do—and I mean it." " Ha, ha, ha,—you little know of my power if you think you can thwart me in my purpose. I tell thee, as sure as the God of heaven lives, you shall be my wife." "No, no. Before heaven I protest against such, unholy union. You can not have my heart, and such.unfon would be but foul mockery." "Oho—now you come to the point. I can't have your heart, eh ? Perhaps your heart is given to the gun-maker ?" Rosalind's eyes flashed in an instant. The words qf the duke were spoken sneeringly and contemp- tuously, and they jarred upon the young girl's soul. "Aye," she quickly uttered, and boldly, too, "I do love Rune Nevel ; and he is worthy of my love." "Now, my pretty ward," resumed Olga, in a tone of peculiar irony, "you have spoken as r hoped you would speak—plainly, and to the point: ao I can answer just as plainly. Know, then, that Rune Nevel can never he your husband. He stands Charged with a horrid crime, and the Emperor only waits to see whether the count recovers or not ere he awards the punishment. The gun-maker is for- bidden, on pain of death, to leave the city. So you may cast him from your thoughts as soon as pos- sible." "What crime is Runic accused of?" the maiden aeked. "Of murder." "In wounding the count ?" "Yes." "Oh, how can you bring your. tongue to such speech? You know the noble youth was not to blame in this affair. He was—" "Hold, Rosalind. I want no argument on this question. You have heard what I have said, and be assured that I mean it. I had hoped you would re- ceive my proposal with more favour; but I did not enter into the plan until my mind was all made up, and the thing all fixed. You will become my wife within one month!" "I will flee to the Emperor," gasped Rosalind. "You will not leave this palace again until you are the Duchess of Tale!" "I will never speak the word that is necessary to make me your wife—never! At the altar, if you be by my side, my lips shall be sealed, and no power on earth shall loose them !" "Do you mean this ?"Avhispered the duke. "As God lives, I do." "Then mark me": the stout, dark nobleman gazed fixedly into the maiden's face as he spoke, and in his look and tone there was a fiendish ex- pression which could not be mistaken—" I shall dp all in my power towards making you my lawfdl. wife ; but if you will not do this, then you shall be that ether thing I Mine thou art and shall be while we both do live. I'll own thee—l'll possess thy body, and I'll make thee a curse to thyself! If you will not speak that word—if you will not let the priest marry us as I have purposed, then .you shall become what I have the power to make thee with- out the speaking of that mutual pledge. Mark me. for I am in earnest—" Here the duke arose and clenched his hands. His brow was marked with passion, and his lips were compressed. 1118 eye burned with a fierce fire. and in every way did he look the man whb stakes his soul, and defies Satan to the combat. "Rosalind Valdai," lie hissed," "my bed shall be your bed! My will shall be your master! My lust shall feed upon your charms, and your body shall only minister to my passions! I'll use thee—use thee as I list—and when I tire of thee I'll cast thee out into the streets for dogs to bark at; for men to sneer at; and for all honest women to shun! So will Ido if you' become not -my wife! God in heaven witness !" With one deep, soul-dying moan, the poor girl sank down shivering and pale. The duke caught her as she fell, and having laid lier senseless form back upon the couch he strode from the apartment. (To be continued.)

div.head: IMPERIAL P.A.B.LIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL P.A.B.LIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS, MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at half-past four o'clock. Buss ADVANCED.—The Transfer of Railways (Ireland) Bill was read a third time. Lord DEMEAN moved the second reading of the Duration of Speeches Bill, but the motion was negatived, A number Of Bills were advanced a stage, and the House adjourned at ten minutes to five HOUSE OF COMMONS, MONDAY. The Deputy Speaker took the chair at three o'clock, and it was notiCeable that the newly constituted Irish party was early in attendance and took possession of the seats formerly occupied by Mr. Parnell and his friends. NEW WRIT.—A new writ was issued for North Kil- kenny, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Marum. LIVERPOOL Posr OFFICE.—Mr. RATERS, replying to Sir G. Baden-Powell, said additional accommodation was required at the Liverpool Post Office, and a specal in- quiry would be made into the subject. JUDICIAL RENTS.—MT. BALFOUR, in answer to Mr. J. M'Carthy, said that under the Land Act, 1887, the modi- fication of judicial rents depended upon the fall of prices, and as the prices of potatoes had risen the' rents should also be increased. • 'SEED POTATO BILL.—The Seed Potatoes Bill was read a third time. bum LIND Bit.—Mr. BALFOUR formally moved the second reading of the Land Department (Ireland) Bill.— Mr. HEALEY protested against such an important mea- sure being rushed through the House, and moved the adjournment of debate, which he ultimately withdretv. He afterwards criticised the measure at some length.— The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for Ireland said Mr. Healey had adduced no arguments why the measure should not be read a second time.—Sir G. TREVELYAN said the Bill was land purchased exclusively by the State, from which he apprehended strained relationship between the two countries.—Mr. T. W. RUSSELL expressed general apprlval of the Bill.—Mr. BALFOUR having replied to the - various criticisms passed on the measure, it was read a second time amid cheers. The House adjmrned at 7.5 HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at twenty minutes to eleven o'clock. HURRIED LEGISLATION. —The Seed Potatoes Supply (Ireland) Bill was read a second time, on the motion of Lord CADOGAN, and, the standing orders having been suspended, passed through its remaining stages. The Hares Preservation Bill and the Archdeaconry of Corn- wall Bill were read a third time, and passed, and the sitting was then suspended, the business having occupied five minutes. Their lordships reassembled at four o'clock, when the Lord Chancellor, the Earl of Limerick, and the Earl of Mount-Edgcumbe, in their peels' robes of scarlet and ermine, took their seats as Royal Commis- sioners on a bench placed in front of the throne. The only other peers present were the Duke of Bedford and Lord Norton. The Commissioners having been sum- moned. the Royal assent was given in the customary form to the Transfer of Railways (Ireland) Act and the Seed Poratoes Supply (Ireland) Act. The House adjourned at a quarter-past four till Thurs- day, the 22nd of January. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAT. The Deputy-Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS, &C.—Mr. Goscirsa informed Mr. Peter Peter M'Donald that the Colonies had not urged him to take any action regarding permission to trustees to invest trust funds in colonial securities.—Mr. MATTHEWS replying to Mr. Cunninghame Graham, professed in- ability to procure a complete return of the number of accidents on the Manchester Ship Canal.—Sir MICHAEL HIS BEACH intimated to Mr. Causton that the Govern- ment had no power to extend the time under the Weights and Measures Act for allowing weighing instruments used in trade to be stamped. Mr. CHAPLIN informed Mr. Ernest Spencer that the Government had not yet received any of Dr. Koch's fluid for the purpose of experiment- inenting upon animals. Replying to Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. W. H. SMITH promised that the report of the Crof- ters Commission on the question of public works would, be carefully considered. Ameng new bills brought in and read a first time was one by Mr. Pitt Lewis for preventing purchasers of stocks from sustaining losses by forged transfers.—Mr. W. H. Syrrrn, replying to Mr. Healey, promised that neither the Land Depart- ment (Ireland) Bill nor the Purchase of Land and Con- gested Districts (Ireland) Bill would be taken until the 29th January.—Mr. SMITH then moved the adjournment of the House to Thursday, January 22nd. Some discus- sion took place regardinz a memorial from tenants on the Tullamore and Lane-Fox estates, who had purchased under the Ashbourne Act, asking for an extension of time, and Mr. Balfour promised to lay some papers on the table.—Mr. MARJORIBANICS gave notice for the 3rd February to call attention to the new magazine rifle, and the House adjourned till the 22nd January. •

div.head: FATAL BLASTING EXPLOSION IN WALES.
div.p: FATAL BLASTING EXPLOSION IN WALES.

, Whilst a gang of workmen were engaged on Monday clearing off the rubbish, after the firing of nine shots at the new Vivian Pit, now being sunk midway between Abertillery and Aberbeeg, Monmouthshire, by Mr. Cole- son, Durham, an unexploded shot fired, blowing to pieces the man named Banister, whose shovel had accidentally struck it. Another man named Thomas Rees, who also received the force of the explosion, was blown some dis- tance and killed on the spot, and George Nellard, who stood war, was alsa so badly injured that his case is al- most hopeless. Six other Englishmen, were also injured and are now under medical treatment.

div.head: RAILWAY RATES- AND CHARGES.
div.p: RAILWAY RATES- AND CHARGES.

The President of the Board of Trade received a depu- tation on Wednesday from the Lancashire and Cheshire Conference on Railway Rates and Charges, who desired to urge that the railway companies should be required to furnish fuller information in reference to their contention that the classification and schedule of maximum rates proposed by the Board of Trade would involve a loss of revenue to the companies. Sir John Harwood having stated the claims of the traders to be supplied with his information, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach said that if other districts made the same demand the returns would ex- tend to millions of tates. Mr. Marshall Stephens said the thousands of articles aiven in the classification of merchandise were governed as to rates by certain typical articles, and these the President of the Board of Trade had before him. Sir Michael said that what he could fairly ask for he would ask for. He could not, however, ask for things which he believed could not be furnished for months, and it was necessary in the general interest that Parliament should deal with the matter In the coming session. Eventually Mr. Tomlinson, M.P., suggested that a representative of the traders should meet a repre- sentative of the railway companies and a representative of the Board of Trade with a view to examining the list and considering what limitations were practicable, and this was agreed to.
MR. GLADSTONE, AND LABOUR REPRESENTATION. • Mr. S. Woods, the Labour candidate for the Ince Division, has received the following letter from Mr. Glad-

'Stone Dear Sir,—You may be aware that I feel a good deal of difficulty, as a general rule, in giving an opinion or expressing a wish as to the SlleeeSs of any particular can- didate on the Liberal side, for fret I should appear to be officiously prejudg,ing, the case for the constituency. But, having given full consideration to the terms of the 'letter which you did Me the honour to address to me some weeks ago, I now feel justified in stating to you that I ehould heartily rejoice in your being returned to • Parliament. I should welcome your accession to the ranks of those who, with daily brightening prospects, sustain in the House of Commons the great Imperial in- terests involved in the Irish cause ; and I Mould also regard with particular interest the addition to be made in your person not only to the sup- porters of Liberal principles but to the special representa- tion of labour in Parliament. This represention. com- paratively new in our history, has obtained additional scowi since the Franchise Act of 1884, and has proved most valuable, alike 'Mr the special purpose of giving voice and weight to the needs, views, and wishes of labour, and for the more general end of thoroughly adapting Parliament for the fulfilment of its varied duties. But, together with my friends, lam of opinion that the representation of labour has not yet been carried far enough, and that the benefits it has produced will be more fully reaped if an increase takes place in the number of seats, held by this valuable class of members. Such an increaS4 ought to incite no alarm on the part of other classes. t,ought, on the contrary, to give satis- faction to all who desire that the questions to be dis- cussed in Parliament shonld enjoy all the advantage that can be derived from having lights thrown upon them% from every quarter. We have testified in various parts of the country our desire to enjoy this aid to good legis- lation and administration, and I act on a similar principle in your individual case, as Tern given to understand that the Ince Division is one well suited to return a Labour candidate possessed. like yourself, of the general cenfid- mice of the mining and artisan population.-1 remain, dear sir, your faithful and obedient W. E. GLADSTONE. S. WOOdSIESq*
