div.head: MR. P A.RNELL DEPOSED.
div.p: MR. P A.RNELL DEPOSED.

A DIVIDED PARTY. ' At the resumed meeting of the Irish party on Saturday, after some warm personal discussion, the report of the Committee appointed to confer with Mr. Gladstone was read. It embodied letters from Mr. John Morley and Sir W. Harcourt, both of whom intimated that the question submitted was for Mr. Gladstone alone to decide. The deputation, it was stated, then sought an interview with Mr. Gladstone on the basis laid down respecting the con- trol of the constabulary and dealing with the land ques- tion. Mr. Gladstone was reported to have said that while he was willing at all times to confer with the Irish members on questions affecting their country, such a conference was barred when it was sought for the de- clared purpose of determining a question of recollection as to the Hawarden conversation. The question raised by his letter to Mr. Morley was a question of leadership, representing what he found to be the views of the Liberal party of Great Britain and having no connection with Home Rule or its conditions. The British Liberal party was enthusiastic for Home Rule, but the trust which it had committed to him did not authorize him to open such a discussion in connection with the question of leader- ship, on which they entertained a separate and decided opinion. After this the deputation sought another interview with the Liberal leader, but were informed that Mr. Gladstone could not undertake to make any statement of the intentions of himself and his colleagues on the matters referred to or on any other provions of a Home Rule Bill, in connection with-a dispute about the leader- ship of the Irish party. Mr. Gladstone further 'inti- mated that when that question was disposed of in a way which would enable former relations to be renewed, it would be his duty to enter without prejudice into con- fidential communication upon all amendments of parti- culars and suggestions for improvement of any plan for "Home Rule. He anticipated that In present circum- stances the deputation would agree with him that there would be no advantage in a further personal interview. An acrimonious discussion followed the reading of the report, and in the end forty-five members Including Mr. J. H. M'Carthy, who on a former occasion, voted for Mr. Parnell, left the meeting. Mr. Parnell and his friends remained in conference for some time, and passed a reso- lution calling the attention of their countrymen to the attitude of Mr. Gladstone. The majority assembled in another room, where they adopted resolutions deposing Mr. Parnell, electing Mr. Justin M'Carthy as his successor to act with eight mem- bers of the party who will be nominated by ballot, and pledging the party to remain an independent Irish party, and to accept no measure of Home Rule that will not satisfy the aspirations of the Irish race. A meeting at which about two thousand persons were present, was held on Sunday, in Phtenix Park, Dublin, to exprese confidence in Mr. Parnell. A number of speeches were made, including one by th 3 Lord Mayor, and resolutions were passed condemning the action of , the members for thd city who had voted- against Mr. Parnell, and setting ferth the opinion of the meeting that Mi. Parnell alone was fitted to lead the Irish nation. Following Mass, on Sunday, at Douglas, a suburb of Cork, in Mr. Parnell's constituench. a small meeting of members of the National League was held, at which the Rev. Canon Murray spoke strongly against the retention by Mr. Parnell of the leadership Of the Irish party. A resolution accordance with the Rev. Canon's views was passed. The manifesto of the Archbishops and Bishops was read in many of the Roman Catholic churches of Ireland on Sunday, and in a large number of cases refe- rences were made from the pulpit supporting the action taken by the hierarchy. Nearly all the Nationalist branches in Liverpool passed resolutions on Sunday hostile to Mr. Parnell. Resolu- tions, some favourable but more hostile, are still being passed in different parts of the country. The" Freeman's Journal" says the O'Gorman Mahon has declared against Mr. Parnell. MR. GLADSTONE'S VIEW. Mr. Gladstone, replying to an address from the con- veners of the Midlothian Liberal Committee,.writes, un- der Monday's date, that "at present there appears to be no question affecting himself, but only an unexplained contradiction between Mr. Parnell and Mr. Parnell—be- tween the Mr. Parnell of November, 1890, and the Mr. Parnell of all former dates since the i4teevie3v at Hawar- den." •

A NEW WHIP, Ste. One of the most serious losses the Irish Parliamentary Party suffer by-the recent splitting-up is that of the services of Mr. Richard Power as whip. Mr. 'Power is popular in all parts of the House and has had long experience in the office as Whip. Sir Thomas Esmonde has been selected to fill the vacancy, Mr. Deasy acting as First Whip. Mr. Parnell was deposed from the leader- ship on Saturday last by 45 votes. Mr. B. W. Soper, Loudwater, Bucks, calls attention to the curious coin- cidence that on the 17th May, 1880, ten-and-a-half years ago: Mr. Parnell was elected chairman of the party by 45 votes. The fact is on record in " Haydn's Diction- ary of Dates." FEATURES OF THE SPLIT. Looking down the list of Irish members who have gone with Mr. Parnell, and those who stand with the majority for Home Rule, it is significant to note that of twenty-five who have suffered imprisonment under Mr. • Balfour's Acts only seven are to be found in Mr. Par- nell's party, the remaining eighteen going with the majority. It is understood that of the Irish representa- tives hitherto under the leadership of Mr. Parnell, forty-four have been in receipt of money drawn from the party funds. Of these, eleven remain with Mr. Par- nell, not less than thirty-three testifying to their single- ness of purpose by going with the Heine Rule party. Of the twelve Irish members who are Protestants no fewer than eight have ranged themselves with the party op- posed to Mr. Parnell. They are Mr. Abraham, Mr. T. A. Dickson, Mr. Jordan, Mr. Knox, Mr. Swift Mac Neill, Mr. Pinkerton, Dr. Tanner, and Mr. Alfred Webb. On the other side Mr. Parnell, himself a Protestant, can still count on the support of three co-religionists—Mr. W. A. Macdonald, now the only blind member of the House of Commons • Mr. Pierce Mahony, who was formerly an Assist aat frish,Land Commiasioner, and Mr. Henry Flar- rison, who lately fignred in the proceedings at Tip- perary. FUNDS AND A NEVVSPAPER. The main financial kesources of the Irish party are vested in the French Funcis,and it is probable that litiga- tion will arise in the French Courts as to their disposition. The popular idea that Mr. Parnell is sole a rlaiter of the money is, we believe, entirely erroneous. There is a sum of about £20,000 which Mr. Paxnell may draw upon over his own siznature; but the great bulk of the money can be made available only by a concurrence of signatures impossible in present circumstances. The Rroposal to start a new paper in Dublin in the interests of the Home Rule Parliamentary party on Mon- day received promises ctsupport which place the affairs on a business footing. It is intended to form a joint- stock company, with a capital of £lOO,OOO, in shares, of which 10s. will be forthwith called up. The necessary amount has, we learn, already been almost fully sub- scribed. ---- • ---

div.head: MR. PARNELL VISITS IRELAND.
div.p: MR. PARNELL VISITS IRELAND.
"UNITED IRELAND" SEIZED.

Mr. Parnell arrived at Kingstown Harbour from Lon- don at an early hour on Wednesday morning, and was the recipient of somewhat mixed attentions from the Crowd, though his reception by his own supporters was of an enthusiastic character. Replying to an address from the Nationalists of the place, Mr. Parnell. expressed himself confident of victory. An address was also pre- sented at 13ray. The chief event of the day, however. was Mr. Parnell's visit to the offices of" United Ireland," which he seized with the aid of Mr. J. Clancy, sub- sheriff, and his officers, several of Mr. Parnell's following being present. Mr. Bodkin was summarily dismissed from his post of assistant editor, and, after he had left the building, an energetic combat took place between the sub-sheriff's men and certain clerks in the commer- cial department. The current issue of " United Ireland," containing letters and articles against Mr. Parnell, was confiscated and destroyed. In the evening a great meet- ing of Mr. Parnell's friends was held in the Rotundo amid scents of the • greatest turbulence, owing to the enormous crowds who fought their way from the street into the build- ing. Mr. Parnell was conducted to the Ro- tund° by a to-chlight procession. Responding to a vote of confidence, he declared the movement against him to be one of hypocrisy, of mental aberration, and of invincible ignorance. It was thought there was no other side, but his defence would be known some day. The issue raised meant the life or death of the constitu- tional movement, and if that movement was surendered or discredited England would find herself face to face with that imperishable force which that night gave him vitality and power. He proclaimed his invincible de- termination to continue in the path of the past sixteen years. The "New York World" publishes an inter- view with Mr. Parnell at the House of Commons, in the course of which he went into the recent negotiations,and in reply to a direct question, emphatically contradicted Davitt's statement that he had ever discussed the divorce business with him, or had stated that he would clear away the charges. THE NORTH KILKENNY VACANCY.

Active preparations are being made for the pending election in the place of the late Mr. Marum, M.P., the writ for which has been issued. Sir J. Pope Hennessey, who had been adopted as the Nationalist candidate, and respecting whom sane doubt was entertained until Tues- day as to whether he u as a Parnellite or anti-Parnellite, has declared that as a Roman Catholic he cannot go against the wishes of his bishops, and he has since tele- graphed to Kilkenny declaring his adhesion to Mr. Justice M`Carthy as the leader of the party. A meeting of the priests of Kilkenny was held in that town on Tuesday to consider the political situation, and a resolution was un- animously passed supporting Mr. M'Carthy and the majority of the Irish party. It is probable that within a short time there will be two elections for the county Kilkenny. The writ for North Kilkenny was moved on Monday. The member for South Kilkenny, is Mr. Chance, a well-known solicitor in Dublin, who finds the necessity of attendance at West-

minster incompatible with his professional interests, and desires to be relieved of his Parliamentary duties. Mr. Chance is a strong opponent of Mr. Parnell, but he be- lieves the seat to be a perfectly safe one. The writ could not be issued during the recess. The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in North Kilkenny has been fixed for December 15 and the polling for the 22nd. Mr. Vincent Scully, who has decided to stand for North Kilkenny at Mr. Parnell's request, arrived there on Thursday, and issued his election address. Sir John Pope Hennessey, the anti-Parnellite candidate, also ar- rived there on Thursday. There was considerable ex- citement and some violent scenes.

div.head: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 131 1890.
div.p: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 131 1890.

I up an especially appropriate prayer, after which • an address was delivered by the Rev. J. Yonge. • In - the course of his .remarks Mr. Yonge said_lt could never be an easy matter to speak upon an occa- sion like that, the halt was too full, and the time L was too short; and yet to withhold some measure . of. speech would be unjust alike to the memory of the dead, and to the requirements of the living. It was fitting,therefore, that words should be spoken, how- ever of necessity, broken and halting they might be. Their beloved and honoured. friend, Samuel Rigby, was not in the narrow housebn which, that day, they gazed with saddened hearts. For ever he had left behind him the transient and the perishable, and had gone forward, upward, to inheritance, the enterprise, and the blessed- ness of the Saint), in light. Monist upon their own account, they might; and none of them who knew him could help it. But mourn for him they could not. The representative character of that assembly was testimony that their friend's death had touched nearly all sorts and conditions of men. Warrington was conscious of a public loss, and its people mourned their bereavement of a personal friend. Genial, thoughtful, kind, courteous to all, Mr. Rigby lived to awaken a friendly smile upon every face, and to send a ray of cheery sunshine into every heart. It was such ,a life alone that could secure such a farewell from earth as this. When business arrangements led their friend to make his home in Warrington, he gave evidence from the first that he had at heart the welfare of others, quite as thoroughly as any interests of his own. He came to follow here the kind of career which his beliefs and desires and sympathies had ever led him to pursue from his youth. He came to live a useful life, and right well had he done it. He was diligent in busi- ness ; making full use of considerable business aptitudes, showing large tact in the guidance and control of those who worked with and for him ; resolute, no doubt, in carrying out and making others carry out, what he believed right and good, and yet hardly ever failing to be considerate and kindly, even in the exercise of that delicate and difficult duty of a large employer—personal government. Having a generous and unselfish nature, and living, moreover, under the inspiration of Christian faith and principle, he gladly used his means to brighten other lives, to supply their needs, and to further true and humane and Christian enterprise. Coming to War- rington, Mr. Rigby at once went to the Wycliffe Chapel, and cast in his lot with the people he found there. He doubted whether any one would grudge or deny the statement that that Chapel was Mr. Rigby's monu- ment in this town. A conscientious Nonconformist and Congregationalist, he laid himself out from the beginn- ing to uplift the church and denomination to which he adhered. Every church, not only free, but established, shared in his sympathy and practical help. If he con- tributed to build the tower of Wycliffe, he contributed also to the erection of the steeple of St. Stephen's, and every cause, religious, educational, philanthropic, and social, found him a wise counseller, and a liberal spirit. Mr. Rigby took an earnest and enthusiastic part in politics. Be believed that the religious life did not ab- solve from political work, but involved it. His political principles,aSalso his ecclesiastical ones,he held from earn- est conscientious conviction; and he knew how to hold and advocate his own against all corners. The churches in Manchester, Bowdon, Warrington, and Chester, with which he had been identified, would recollect his assi- duous regularity at worships his unfluctuating indus- try in work ; his devout and manly utterances in prayer; his wise and stimulating counsels, and his con- sistent Christian example. And if thus their friend's life left its indelible impression upon the community at large, how unspeakably noble and precious must be his memory to all in the inner and sacred circle of his family and home. They might not intrude into that domain, even in quest of what might be beautiful to discover, Itnd profitable to study ; but if they, who had known him so principally in his more public and social capaci- ties, had so keen a sense of loss in his death, they could better imagine their larger sense, and the more truly ex- tend to them their respectful sympathy. In conclusion, the rev, gentleman said they wept bescause this side the river they could see Mr. Rigby's face no more; but they rejoiced in the confident and assured hope that again they would meet, and clasp inseparable hands upon the eternal shore. Immediately after the service, a procession was formed in Bewsey-street. It was headed by several members of the police force and the Mayor and mem- bers of the Corporation, who were followed by repre- sentatives of the Warrington Liberal Association, the employ& of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby's from the mills at Manchester and Warrington, Chester friends and deputations, and deacons and members of the Wycliffe Church. Then came a carriage of officiating ministers, and the hearse, • through the glass sides of which the coffin and the wreaths which had been placed upon it could be seen. Then followed 22 private carriages, containing relatives of the deceased and others. Many blinds were lowered as the procession passed on its way to the cemetery, the route thither being lined with spec- tators. A large number of persons had assembled in the cemetery to witness, the funeral obsequies there, and the remains of the late Mr. Rigby were lowered into the family vault (which is situate a few yards on the east side of the fottntain) amid every demonstration of respect. The ceremony at the grave, which only occupied a few minutes, was performed by the Rev. Professor Armitage, M.A. The whole of the funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. Bailey on behalf of Messrs. Brown, Holmes, and Co., of Chester, by whom the coffin, which bore the simple inscription of the date of birth and death of the deceased, Was supplied. The following is a list of th 3 ladies and gentlemen who had forwarded wreaths :—The widow; the choir of Northgate Congregational Chufch ; the President and Executive Committee of the Manchester Steam Users As- sociation; the Rev. F. Barnes and the deacons of North

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR S. RIGBY.
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR S. RIGBY.

The funeral of the late Mr. S. Rigby, which took place on Saturday, was, in its way, a most impressive testi- mony of the esteem of all clauses of people which the deceased gentleman had won during his life time. The remains were brought by rail on Saturday morning from Fern Bank, Liverpool-road, Chester, where the death took place, to Warrington, and at one o'clock a funeral service was held in Wycliffe Church, at which there was a large attendance. At Chester there was a procession from Fern Bank to the station. The mourners were chie- fly on foot, the four broughams which formed: the only exception being occupied as under:—First brougham,' Mrs. Rigby, Mr. Ziba Armitage, Mrs. Brinsley, and Mr. W. Kershaw' Second brougham, Mrs. John Rigby, Mrs. Kershaw, Mrs, Townsend, and Mr. Herbert Kershaw. Third brougham, Rev. F. Barnes, Dr. Thomas" and Mr. H. T. Brown. Fourth brougham, (the private convey- ance of his Worship), the Mayor of Chester, (Alderman Charles Brown) and Dr. Davies-Colley. The pedestrian portion of the procession which preceded the hearse and , mourning coaches was led by Mr. William Brown (chair- ' man) and the members of the Free Library Committee, and was constituted as follows :—Messrs. G. R. Griffith, Thomas Shepherd, W. Shone, F. F. Brown, and Dr. Stolterfoth • representing the Chester School of Science and Art), Revs. J. Margan,J. W.Clarke,W. Jones. Thorn- ton, J. K. Montgomery, W. Bainbridge, John Roberts, Mr. C. C. Bowlet and Mr A. C. Gornall (representing the Chester City Mission), Messrs,. J. Greenhalgh (agent), R. Burrows, and W. Pixton (of the Chester Liberal Club), and Messrs. George Day, J. D. Bowers, B. Adams, J. Okell, G. E. Clarke, G. Sayce, R. Jackson, John Powell, J. Jackson, J. Skeldon, G. Haswell, F. Ashby, W. H. Denson, and Lewis. On the route from Liverpool-read to the station blinds were drawn in nearly every house, and shutters on the windows of the tradesmen in the neighbourhood presented a similar token et respect. On arrival at the station a small crowd had gathered to wit- ness the placing of the coffin in the 11.55 train to Warrington. The service at Wycliffe Chapel was held at one o'clock and amongst these present were :—Mrs. Rigby (widow), Mrs. John Rigby, Mrs. Brinsley, Mrs. Kershaw, Mr. and Mrs. William Armitage, Mr. and,Mrs Z. Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. William Armitage, jun., Mr. J. R. Stainforth, Mr. and Mrs. W. Rigby, Rev. E. Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. Jesse Haworth, Mr. W. Oswald Carver, Mr. and Mrs. S. Marshall Bulley, Mr. Charles Townsend, Mr. Walter Kerehaw, Mr. Herbert Kershaw, Mr. and Mrs. G. F. Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. S. Rigby Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Simpson, Mr. John Rigby, Mr. Marshall Rigby, Mr. J. Frederick Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. Pearce, Mr. William Milne, and Mr. Herbert Spencer. Mr. Henry Lee and Mr. J. E. Fletcher repre- sented the Steam Users' Association, and Messrs. W. E. Melland, John Mills, Joseph Davies, J.P., the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank, with Mr. J. H. S. Crompton, the general manager, Mr. H. T. Brown, Chester, Dr. Thomas and the Rev. F. Barnes, 8.A., of Chester, were also present, in addition to the Rev. John Yonge (pastor of Wycliffe Congregatiocal Church), and the Rev. Professor Armitage, M.A., of Bradford. The Corporation were re: presented by the Mayor (who wore his chain of office which was draped for the occasion), - Aldermen Sutton Burgess, and Wright; Councillors R. T. Fairclough, H. Roberts, Shaw Green, S. J. Beaman, J. Muir, J. Garner, J. H. Fleming, T. Hutchinson, F. W. Monks, and James Hill ; Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. Charles Chorley (borough treasurer), Mr. T. Longdin (boeough surveyor), and Mr. George F. F. White (assistant magistrates' clerk.) The workpeople of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby's (Manchester and Warring- ton) were represented by the following: Warrington, Messrs. D. Baillie. P. T. Wiuskill, W. T. Smitners, C. Hibbert, and John Lingard ; Manchester, Messrs. G. H. Adshead, T. H. Glendinning, Thomas Wilshaw, S. • Butler, Samuel Wardleworth, John Edelston, John Roberts, Robert Booth, and W. Gee. Among others in the church were—The Revs. S. Wilkinson, John Gunnell, T. Ross, J. Warnock, Edward Moore, W. Graham, Charles Clay, B.A. (Lymm) ; and Messrs. Robert Gar- nett, F. Monks, Thomas Morris, Dr. Gornall, Richard Roberts, William Roberts, Edwin Richardson, Thomas Rigby (late Secretary of the Royal Manchester, Liver. pool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society), John Dignum, John Walker, W. Roberts, Charles Twiss, T. Wallington, J. R. Buckton, (magitarates' clerk for the Newton Petty Sessional Division), H. Greenall, J. S. Garland, John Hough, (Widnes), William Grimshaw, Samuel Jones, England, Legge James Strange, S. B. Stringer William Diggle, Dia (former coachman of the deceased), Mitchell (manager of the Liberal Club), , John Harrison, and A. Rathbone. The service that waslield in the chapel was simple but impressive. The coffin was placed within the com- munion rail and was almost covered with wreaths. While the congregation were taking their seats the , organist played suitable music on the organ. The service opened with the singing of the well-known hymn beginning with the line "Brief life is here our portion," and then the lesson was read by the Rev. F. Barnes, of Chester. The same minister offered

gate Church; the workpecple of Cockhedge Mills, War- rington ; the nephews and nieces,residing at Altrincham ; Miss Rougier, Mrs. James H. Kershaw and family, Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Miss Barclay, Alderman and Mrs. Burgess, Alderman and Mrs. Davies, Mr. and Mrs. T. F. Denson, Mr. Ledsham and family, Mrs. John Rigby and family, Mr. and Mrs. A. J. Pearce, Mrs. Drury, Mr. R. C. Drury, the Rev. J. and Mrs. Yonge, Mr. and Mrs. Jesse Haworth (Bowdon), and Miss Appleton. There were several other wreaths to which no names had been affixed. • MEMORIAL SERMON. A memorial sermon for thelate MK Samuel pjgby was preached in the Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening, by the Rev. John Yonge. The preacher took tor his text "Faithful unto death," and during thesourse of his ser- mon he described the religious faithfulness of the deceased gentleman, and remarked that the consequence Of Mr. Rigby's faithful observance of public worship was that it came to be to him one of his very choicest de- lights. He enjoyed the services of the sanctuary and got the good out of them. He (the preacher) thought that their friend was very exemplary to their older people, in the fact that he did not constantly plead his years as so many reasons for inactivity, and evidently he preferred to die in harness than to live in inaction. Mr. Rigby was never ashamed of his Nonconformity, rather he boasted somewhat of it, and told his church friends that if they only knew what was good, they would be Nonconformists also, and this was always said with that characteristic pleasantry which might propitiate, but it could never offend. Their parted friend's staunch fidelity to principle had been also seen in his fearless ad- herence to his political party. Never had he showed him- self in any sense a trimmer ; his vote had never been doubt- ful; his opinions in any political crisis had never been ,open to question. A Liberal from conviction, he followed with confidence all truly Liberal politics, believing that all such led in the path of right, progress, and national good. Closing his very able sermon, the Rev. J. Yonge said it was a great responsibility to have known such men; to have had them in our midst, with their energy and industry, and generosity in Christ's service. That Church owed more than could be said, to the life, the love, and the labours of their friend. "Re being dead, yet speaketh." He spoke in that building itself, which he had so largely helped to raise. He spoke in that organ which at the time anonymously he paid for. His pew, to those of them who remembered his habitual presence in it, would always seem to have vision of his form. Samuel Rigby was not likely to be forgetten. He was" Faith- ful unto death" ; staunch, persistent,. true and loyal ; earnest in his faith to God ; in his belief in prayer ; in his value of sanctuary and Sabbath and ordinances.

div.p: 1 SPLENDID GIFT.

Colonel Seeley, commanding the Robin Hood Rifles, the present High Sheriff of Nottingham, and formerly member of Parliament for the borough, has given £lO,OOO towards establishing convalescent homes and a hospital for poor folk in Nottingham.

div.head: SUPPOSED MURDER IN IRELAND.
div.p: SUPPOSED MURDER IN IRELAND.

A Waterford telegram reports that the poitce are in- vestigating the circumstances connected with the mysterious disappearance recently of two farmers while returning from fairs in the county with considerable sums realised by the sale of cattle. It is believed that both men were robbed and murdered, and their bodies buried in order to conceal all evidence of the crimes.

At York Assizes, on Tuesday, Robert Kitching, market gardener, was sentenced to death fof the murder of Police-Sergeant Weedy, at Leeming, near Bedale, York- shire. Prisoner had a spite against the officer, and in September last threatened to shoot him. The same night he armed himself with a gun, and shot Weedy dead. He afterwards obtained the assistance of his brother-in-law to remove the body from his premises to the road.

SHOCKING ICE ACCIDENT. SIX LIVES LOST. A terrible accident, by which six children lost their lives, occurred about six o'clock on Tuesday night, at Tipton, South Staffordshire. A number of school ctil- dren were sliding on an old colliery pool, when the ice broke and eight of them were immersed. Two were rescued, but the other six, whose ages ranged from six to ten years, were drowned. Assistance was promptly at hand, and medical men tried for an hour to restore consciousness, but without avail. All thechildren resided near Dudley.

SHOCKING MURDER OF A BROTaER

, About four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon two brothers,. named Edwin and James OatesTsonsofir farmer residing at Sancreed, near St. Just Cornwalt.'were filling a cart from a manure, heap on the moor about 200 yards from their home, when, without, so far as is known any pro- vocation, Edwin struck his brother a terrific blow over the head with a shovel, knocking him senseless to. the ground. While James lay on the ground Edwin pro- duced a razir, which he had evidently secreted for the purpose, and cut his brother's throat in such a manner as almost to sever his head from the body. Having closed the razor and thrown it away, he returned to his home, where he ate a hearty meal, and talked wilily to his mother as if nothing had happened, remarking in answer to a question that he had left his brother on the moor. His father, on returning to the house and seeing, blood on his aon's hands, hec,ame alarmed, and rushing out on the moor, discovered the dead body of his son James, whose head was frightfully beaten and dis- figured. The razor was found near the body. It is stated that the two brothers were on the most affection- able terms, but Edwin had been noticed lately to be act- ing somewhat strangely, and it is believed that he committed the act in a fit of insanity. He was arrested on Tuesday night and taken to Penzance.

div.head: GENERAL BOOTHS SCHEME.
div.p: GENERAL BOOTHS SCHEME.
VISIT TO ST. HELENS.

On Monday afternoon a deputation of clergymen, ministers, and local gentlemen waited upon the Mayor (Councillor E. Johnson), at the Town Hall, and presented requisitions asking his worship to convene and preside over a representative confer- ence in St. Helens on Wednesday next, on the occa- sion of a visit from General Booth in connection with the promulgation of his scheme of social salva- tion. The deputation was introduced by the Rev. R. J. Ward (Congregational), who handed to his worship two memorials, one signed by local philan- thropic laymen, and the other bearing the names of local clerymen and ministers. Mr. Ward intimated that they had not come to discuss the merits of the scheme, but the interest in the scheme was so general and univer- sal, that they were anxious for his worship to give the conference a representative and public character.—The Mayor said he felt a great deal of difficulty about the matter introduced by the influential deputation. He must not be accused of considering the matter lightly, for he had given it most careful consideration and had come to the conclusion that it was not a matter for him to take up officially as Mayor, or formunicipal machinery to be called into action. He was, personally, much in- terested in the scheme, but he thought any official action would be rather premature, and he felt very sorry that he could not see his way to accede to their wishes.— Councillor J. B. Leach said he was sure they sympathised with the Mayor in his difficulties ; and Mr. C. C. White added that those who had signed the requisitions were not necessarily in favour of thescheme, but wereanxious for further information in regard to it. A vote of thanks was then tendered to his worship, on the motion of the Rev. W. W. Spencer, seconded by the Rev. R. J. Ward, and Supported by Mr. J. Hewitt, and the deputation withdrew. A meeting was afterwards hgld inthe Mayor's committee room and arrangements for the proposed con- ference and public meeting were discussed. It was de- vided to ask Colonel D. Gamble, C. 8., to preside at the afternoon gathering, and Colonel W. W. Pilkington.J.P., at night. A committee consisting of the Revs. H. S. Bolton, W. W. Spencer, R. J. Ward, G. Lakemad, Father Brown Captain dadden (Salvation Army), and Messrs. J. B. Leach, J. Boydell, C. J. Bishop, and F. Dromgoole was appointed to carry out the details.

div.head: DEATH OF LORD TOLLEMACIIE.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD TOLLEMACIIE.

Lord Tollemache of Peckforton Castle, Cheshire, and of Helmingham Hall, Suffolk, died on Tuesday night. Lord Tollemache attained his eighty-fifth birthday on Sunday last, and the occasion was one of congratulation on the extensive Cheshire estate. Last week Lord Tollemach was in his usual health. On the Thursday he left the castle in a dog-cart for a drive around the estate. Des- pite' the fact that a bitter east wind was blow- ing, Lord Tollemache covered just twenty miles on the exposed road. On returning he complained of feeling very cold, and after a time he went to bed. On Saturday and Sunday Dr. Robinson was in attendance and treated his lordship for a severe chill. On Monday Dr. Elliott, of Chester, was sum- moned in consultation, and every endeavour was made to check the progress of the attack. On Tue- day morning Lord Tollemache's condition was found to be somewhat alarming, but his physical strength was so good that the worst was not antici- pated. Towarda night, however, his vitality began to fail, and he died shortly after ten o'clock. , Lord Tollemache was a son of the late Admiral John Richard Delap Tollemache, of Relmingham, Suffolk, and Peckforton, Cheshire, and was born in 1805. Ile sat for South Cheshire in the Conserva- tive interest from 1841 to 1868 and for West Ches- hire from 1868 to 1872. In 1876 he was • created a peer of the United Kingdom, and received the title of Baron Tollemache, of Helming ham, Suffolk. He was married twice—for the first time in 1826 and again in 1850. His first wife died in 1846. Two sons by the first wife are living and nine sons and one daughter by the second wife. He is succeeded by the Hon. Wibraham Frederick Tollemache, who was born in 1832. The new earl was formerly major of the Ist Cheshire Militia, sat for West Cheshire from 1872 to 1885, and he has been marriVd twice. The first marriage t )ok place in 1838, and the second in 1878. The deceased peer was noted for the careful manage- ment of his estates, and was declared to be the finest practical agriculturist in the country-. Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Joseph Chamberlain have repeatedly directed attention to the consumate skill with which he adminis- tered his two large estates—namely, Helmington, in Suffolk, comprising about 7,090 acres, and Peckforton, in Chesnire, 26,000 acres. Lord Tollemache's action in providing the whole of his cottage tenants with three acres and a cow was the origin of his historic phrase. There are no less than 250 of these cottages on the Peckforton Estate, the majority of whom are most comfortably circumstanced. They utilise a portion of the land for a garden, a portion for grazing and tillage, and they supplement their wages adjacent farms by selling the produce from the cows. By this kindly and thoug,htful means Lord Tollemache effectually solved the labour difficulty on the reckforton estate. The farmers rarely or never lost a labourer occupying one of Lord Tollemachoe's picturesque and comfortable cottages. The relationship between his lordship and the tenant farmers was personal. He knew every tenant on his vast estates and his capabilities. Coming into pos- session of the Peckforton estate in 1840, Lord Tolle- mache devoted himself heart and soul to the work of providing nomesteads on the best sanitary pri,nciples, and the result 3s that his tenants have for years taken the bulk of the prizes in the cheese com- petitions at the county and local dairy shows. Lord Tollemache entertained extremely advanced views in regard to a landlord's r3sponsibility to those on his estate. It was this 9verw helming sense of responsibi- lity, coupled with a thorough knowledge of agriculture that made the Peckforton the splendid estate it to-lay. I Lord Tollemache disliked farms exceeding 200 acres in extent, and he equally disapproved of smaller holdings, contending that a thrifty farmer who would prosper on 200 acres of land would probably fail on only 100 acres.' In order to break up his estate into farms of that size, Lord Tollemache built between fifty and sixty farm- houses at a cost of £148,000. His total expenditure on farm homesteads and new cottages up to 1881 amounted to the enormous sum of £280,004. In all his public and private works, Lord Tellemache had a worthy coadjutor in Mr. Stephen Cawley, his agent, whe had been with him for a lifetime. Lora Tol- lemache was one of the most tolerant of men in religious affairs. He subscribed indiscriminately and liberally to churches and chapels on tie estate. John Wesley, when preaching in Cheshire, used to gather his flock under a pear tree on one of his lordship's farms, and when the old tree was blown down, Lord Tolle- mache took a personal part in replanting it with another tree to commemorate the event. Only on one occasion, and that was thirty years ago, did Lord Tollemache come into conflict with the clergy, and that was at Helmingham. Feeling convinced that it the tenant farmers' and the labourers' children were not better educated they would be left behind in the race of life, his lordship established an excellent mixed school there, and in order that no offence should be given to the consciences of Dissenters, the Church Catechism was ex- cluded from the religious exercises. A strong feeling of caste began to prevail. The tenant farmers threatened to withdraw their children from communion with the children of the labourers. The clergy were suspected by Lord Tollemache of stirring up this unpleasant feeling. It was at this critical juncture that Lord Tollemache sent his own boys to the schools, and what is more, re- tained them there for some considerable period. That, his lordship used naively to add, broke the back of the
_ opposition. The funeral will take place in the family burying ground at Ilelmingham, to-day (Saturday.)

THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. DECEMBER 13. 1890.

The Move ENGLAND is not moving quite as in quickly in the matter of technical Education. and secondary education as her best friends desire; but still she is moving, and it is the duty of all citizens who have at heart the welfare of the country to assist the movement. Lord HARTINGTON was well occupied in London the other day in presiding over a large and repre- sentative conference, which met to consider the best mode of utilising the £740,000 which falls to County Councils as their share of the extra duty on beer and spirits. As President of the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Educa- tion, Lord HAariNoTox had much to say in favour of applying the funds as suggested by Parliament, namely in the support of technical and secondary education. Already several County Councils have decided on that course, and others are likely to be largely influenced by the consensus of opinion as ex- presssed at the Conference that it would be a mis- take to apply the allocated money in any other way. If it went into the general fpnd as so much towards reducing the rates, it is not unlikely that 'the trade," who are complaining about the extra tax, would succeed hereafter in obtaining a reduction to the old level, on the plea that, while they might be called upon to pay an additional tax for a special purpose, it was unfair to tax them solely for the purpose of reducing rates. On the other hand, if the liquor duty, with the sanction of Parliament, is applied to educational purposes,it may be taken for granted that Parliament will see to it that supplies are not hereafter suddenly cut off. A good deal will depend upon the amount of pressure which is brought to bear upon County Councils in the shape of applications for grants. Between thirty and forty local authorities have already availed themselves of the provisions of the Technical In- struction Act ; and we may be sure that these authorities in so far as they form sections of a county will not neglect to apply for a share of the allocated spirit duty. Widnes is amongst the places that have adopted the Act ; Runcorn has the subject under consideration ; and we trust to find that the Town Council of Warrington will, ati their next meeting, show that they aro disposed to I i

put themselves in line with other communities. There is a feeling in the town that the time has come for establishing a Technical School; and it is scarcely necessary to say that, if a substantial annual grant can be obtained from the Lancashire County Council, it will be possible to establish and conduct such a school without its becoming an atipreciable burden upon the rates. Warrington, it must be conceded, is not so favourably situated as to be justified in neglecting to obtain a share of any good thing that is to be had.

Town Councillors and Local Board-men are not as a rule persons who have given special attentioa to the education problem, except in so far as it re- lates to the compulsory attendance of school. , children ; and, as we take it for granted that they as well as other citizens are desirous at the .present time of extending their knowledge of the subject, we have pleasure in making them acquainted with a shilling hand-book prepared by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., and Mr. E. Ellis, M.P., and pub- lished by Mr. John Heywood. The title of the work is " Public Education in Cheshire," but it. gives much valuable information that may be made serviceable in every part of England. There is no work, in fact, that we have yet seen which brings the reader so completely up to date on the education question. The Technical Instruc- tion Act (1889), and the Local Taxation Act.. (1890), are given in full, along with explanatory notes, and along with a chapter on what may be accomplished under these Acts. Other chapters. deal with the Schools and the People: salient. points of the new Education Code; the for- mation of Science and Art Schools and Classes; a. Council of Education for Cheshire; and sugges- tions and recommendations from various educa- tional systems. There is, too, a summary of the law relating te the establishment of Public Libraries, Museums, and Schools of Science, with carefully compiled, Cheshire, statistics with re- gard to the Elementary and Endowed Schools, Board Schools, Science Schools, Public Libraries, &c. It will be seen that no little time and thought have been bestowed upon the pre- paration of the hand-book; and it is to be hoped that a similar work will be issued for Lancashire. It would certainly be of great use, not only to. members of County and other Councils, but to all who are interested in education. It is aptly re- marked, in the section on "The Schools and the People," that "education is cheaper than igno- rance " ; but the truth is not as yet sufficiently - realised, or there would be a loss grudging spirit, displayed in dealing with eduntional matters. It is not, however, from the masses that complaints: come—a. fact which should encourage these is authority who are timidly feeling their, way.. • Another thing: there is plenty of money lying idle which may yet be devoted to educational purposes. Not later than Monday last, the Mastet of the plumbers Company, at a conversazione, London announced that the Company intended to: devote i 290,000 of their funds tospromoting tech- nical and sanitary instruction. This is cheering ;- t we are getting on : all that is necesmr^ is to keep. J pinving, and to accelerate the pace a tittle.

"An IT is seldom that an English judge Abominable feels himself called upon to con- System." demn anything relating to the ad- ministration of the law,in such strong terms as VIT. JUSTICE WILLs used, yesterday week, in connection with a local case tried at the Liverpool Assizes. b. servant girl named Kate Mellitt, aged 17 only, was. charged with burglary at Newton, but the case, completely broke down, the judge remarking that even if it had been proved it would only have been one of simple larceny. A feature which attracted attention was disclosed in the fact that no infor- mation of this so-called burglary was given to the police until a week after the alleged robbery. Mr. JUSTICE Wnaz noticed further that the magistrates' Clerk to the Newton Police Court was also the prosecuting solicitor; and it was a practice of this kind which he characterised as "an abominable system." •

Although (his lordship remarked) he had no ides, of suggesting that it would influence that gentle- man because he was going to have the prosecution. if the prisoner were going to be sent for trial, still he would ask what people would think of his (the judge's) position if he were to get a guinea for every person he convicted, and nothing for persons who were acquitted ? All the prestige and all the traditions which bung about the bench of justice would be shaken if a judge was to get pecuniary benefit out of what lie decided. A magistrates' crerk was almost practically in the position of saying whether a prisoner should be committed or not, for he was cotsulted by the magistrates. He hoped he would live to see the day when such a practice would be prohibited by Act of Parliament.

We are quite sure the public will echo the judge's expression of opinion. Indeed, it will be in the nature of a surprise to most people that such a practice is still carried on outside cities and boroughs. It is a violation of the elementary principles of justice that the legal functionary who has to advise magistrates as to what is to be done with a prisoner, should have an interest in com- mitting him for trial, inasmuch as he can appear at the Assizes and be paid as prosecuting solicitor. It is a glaring anomaly that such a thing should be permitted to magistrates' clerks in counties when it is specially prohibited in boroughs. We take the following as bearing upon the point from Stone's Justices' Manual :

JUSTICES' CLERKS. BOROUGH CLERKS NOT TO PROSECUTE. The Clerk to the Justices shall not, by himself or his partner, or otherwise, be directly or indirectly employed or interested in the prosecution of any offender committed for trial by those justices, or any of them, at any court of gaol delivery or quar- ter sessions. If any person acts in contravention of the last-foregoing provision of this section, he shall for every offence be liable to a fine not exceeding £lOO, recoverable by action. One moiety of any tine so recovered shall, with costs, be paid to the person bringing the action to recover it. (45 and 40 Viet. c. 50 sub-Sects. 3,4, 5.)

. . It will be seen that a borough magistrates' clerk would be liable to a penalty of £lOO for doing what the clerk to the Newton magistrates has done, and.what other magistrates' clerks in the 'counties are in the habit of doing. The difference —and the only difference so far as we can see—is that in one case the "abominable system is toler- ated and in the other it is prohibited. It is to the credit of the members of the legal profession that they are interesting themselves in aiding the agitation which has resulted in the Attorney- General drafting a bill which, if it should pass) will put an end to the anomaly. If Mr. BUCKTON, as clerk to the Newton magistrates, is able to "look before and after" he will take the advice of Mr. JUSTICE WILLS and help the agitation. It cannot be pleasant to be party to a system which, though not as yet illegal, is stigmatised as abom- inable by one of Her Majesty's judges.

On Monday a prisoner named Mullarkey was sentenced to five years penal servitude for stabbing a friend in Widnes, who had sheltered him and his family. It sv„as an instance, as the judge said, of base ingratitude. You take a snake to your bosom and it stings you. There is such a thing as killing for as well as with kindness.

We have received, at the last moment, a letter from out Peuketh Correspondent in which he maintains the accuracy of the summary which he supplied of the paper on Count Tolstoi, and which was questioned by Mr. Peers. The writer of the ipaper (Mr. John •Cxsody) confirms our Correspon- 4ent in stating that the point which Mr. Peers *raphasises was not the gist of the paper.

----- Dr. loch's remedy would appear to have the defects of its merits; it is powerful for mischief as well as good. A servant girl of Innsbruck, stated to be of strong physique, was inoculated for lupus, and died within 36 hours of paralysis of the heart, the reaction being unusually severe. There is evidently something to learn yet in the application of the lymph.

Is there fate in it that the Irt Struggle between the Parnellites and the Irish Parliamentary Party takes place at Kilkenny ? When the Kilkenny cats fought, there was nothing left at the t nish but the tails. It will be quite sufficient if the tussle in the present case results in the disappear- ance of the Parnellite tail.

It is interesting to note that the Tories denounced 4,4 r. Parnell as "too bad to burn" inunediately ,after the Divorce Court proceedings; but since he Jute been set aside for his delinquencies, they have 'changed their tune. Note the following—" The 3,,nagiord Town Commissioners, by six votes to eve, vassal a resolution approving Mr. Parnell's action. uee conservative commissioners voted for the monition." It would seem that the Tories are taking fowl Salisbury's hint to "put their money on Parser

The people, of Warrington will not take Mr. Diggle seriously, and it is a question whether he takes himself seriously. His lectures always resolve themselves into a "screaming farce," which pobody seems to enjoy more than Mr. Diggle. He is to be congratulated on showing himself so lively whgn he is gatting on for eighty. The Howley pept is a nuisanot;, but it doesn't depress him; it ra^A.W. s hint as frisky as if he took whiskey. Ls Liberal Unioni* shouted them- The Tories nd selves hoarse when Mr. Gladstone's Irish Lsnd Bill was before the country, although it was safe- guarded on every side; but they haven't 4 WPfd to say in opposition to Mr. Balfour's Land 13341, which is on worse lines, and deals with over thirty I million* of monei. It has passed the second read- ilig, and will prootak 1:5609M9 147/ and then John Bull will, as Byron has it, "half suspect himself a fool." John will have to pay for his folly,

-- There is something revolting about the way in which the vary worst of criminals become repen- tant when the hangman is at their heels. Here is that ingrained ruffian Macdonald, the brutal mur- derer of the young schoolmistress, writing from gaol to his friends with the fOliowing post_ script of his letter:—" 'Be our sins aS scarlet,' they shall be made whiter than snow,' so says the Scrip- tures," Granted as to some cases, but is it not 7:ssible that in others the scarlet will be found to be a fast dye?

Widnes is about to Apply 101 A, Charter of Incorporation, and there is a difference of opinion as to whether the town should be divided into four wards or six. 'Laving regard to the rapid growth of the town, it would seem that six wards would not be too many. It is one reason for mak- ing the change that there should he fuller repre- sentation of the inhabitants. Widnes should be in the position of the growing.boy who, when he gets a new suit, is supplied with one which leaves!' room to thrive."

At a meeting of Cheshire farmers, on Saturday, one member, said "every man who took a farm over the head of another ought to be boycotted, and ought to be made mincemeat of and harmed as much as possible." He used the word " mince- meat "of course in " a Pickwickian sense." Or can it be that he had a metaphorical eye on the approach of Christmas ? Be that as it may, his brother farmers couldn't tolerate the proposal, which perished amid the cries of "No, no, and. "Shame."

"Mincing," like many other words has more than one mitring. Shakespeare has— I'll turn two mincing steps Into a manly stride." Literally, mincing is the art of chopping meat fine —in preparing for mince pies—and it is with this in mind that Bacon says :—" Mincing of meat as in pies The latest discovery is that mince pies may save the teeth, but they don't save the stomach. Yesterday the Warrington Library and Museum Committee adopted the report of the sub- committee which has had under consideration the subject of Technical Instruction. The - draft scheme to be submitted to the Town Council is based on the supposition that 700 a year will be received from the Lancashire County Council. If less than that sum be obtained, the scheme will of course be altered. It is a case of cutting the coat according to the cloth. We shall give particulars of the proposed scheme in our next Issue.

Perhaps the most singular suicide on record is that of a Kansas girl of seventeen who recently poisoned herself, after a birthday party. " In a note to her mother which was found on the table in her room, she said she wished to die while she was happy, having noticed that older people got more worry than she had." The thought is not new, if the action be. Shakespeare makes" Othello" say in the fervour of his love for " Desdemona "—"lf it were now to die, 't were now to be most happy." Alas and alas, that union ended in murder and suicide.

It is suggestive of the way in which things get mixed that the Sioux Indians are preaching a coming of " TheMessiali," and have amongst them a woman who claims to be "The Mother of Christ." They are looking formircl to a sort of heaven on earth when the whites will cease from troubling, and the herds will be at rest. They have copied some of the early expounders of Christianity in another way in that, whilst looking forward to a period of peace, they threaten to begin with the slaughter of their enemies. The Virgin Mary of the Indians is known, too, as "The Scarlet Woman." Odd, isn't it? General Booth is likely to have a splendid recep- tion when he visits St. Helens on Wednesday next. The Duke of Westminister doesn't approve of the new scheme because it will have a had effect upon existing charities ; but what of that, if it does half the goal that is expected from it? Charities are not an end, but the means to an end. Professor Huxley shows himself severely hostile; he thinks General Booth :should study authorities; but where is there a greater authority on "the sub- merged tenth " than the General? Again, if the scheme should absolutely fail, it willbe something . to have given it a trial, for It tells of duty done, And duty doing.

rho sight of sights in Warrington to-day is at Heath-side (corner of Legh-st.), where three )sets are being built to front the street! There wis one Black Spot before, and the Sanitary Com- mittee's idea of "improvement" is to remove it

Zan d put three in its place. No doubt some sort of .hoarding will be run up finally tohide the ahomina- ition ; but the abomination is there ; and it is a dis- credit to" the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of Warrington." Bye-the-bye, the two working- men members of the Town Council are members of the, Sanitary committee. It would be interest- ing toknow whether they have been party to the erection of these three closets close to, and in a , linewith, the front doors of working-people.

WARNING TO FLATNEN AT RNNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ed ward Haigh, a flatman, was charged with having, on the 18th November, placed the flat Atlantic in such a position on the Bridgewater Canal, at Runcorn, as CO obstruct the free passage of No. 9 and 10 locks, in contravention of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1862. The defendant pleaded guilty, and promised not to offend again, and he was fined £2 including costs. The Manchester Ship Canal Company (bridgewater undertaking) were the prosecu- tors. •

CHILDREN. James Grounds, of Weston Point, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of furious driving. Mr. J. W. Knowles (Widnes), de- fended. Mr. G. Bellamy, printer, St.c., High-st., stated that on the Und November the defendant was driving a horse and cart down High-st. at a furious rate. Two small children were crossing the road at the corner of Lock-st., and had not the ho-se swerved on to the foot- path, they would undoubtedly have been run over. The horse fell and the cart collided with the railings of Roche House (Mrs. Hazlehurst), and broke four iron palings.— Mr. T. Jones, of Leinster Gardens, and P.C. Ratcliffe also deposed that the defendant was driving at a very furious rate.—Mr. Knowles, on behalf of the defendant, denied the furious driving, and contended that the acci- dent occurred solely through defendant pulling up his horse too quickly in order to prevent running over the children. He was merely driving at a steady pace down the street, and this statement was borne out on oath, by Arthur Jones. driver to Messrs. Partington and Lancas- ter, Marshall Hughes, driver to Mr. Welter Collier and another witness. The Bench, however, fined the defen- dant 40s. including costs. DARESBURY SCHOOL BOARD. Mr. Brighouse,County Coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens Town Ball, on Thursday, concerning the death of Annie Burro Ars,aged ten years, daughter of Peter Burrows, labourer, 36, Eccleston-st., St. Helens, who died suddenly on Monday evening, shortly after her return from school. The deceased fell as soon as she got home and vomited frequently, com- plaining of pains in her head. Shortly afterwards the child expired. It appeared that on her way from school the girl fell against a window sill, and Dr. Shannon who made a post-mortem examination as- cribed death to an effusion of blood on the left side of the brain, the result of a fracture on the right temple, which might have been produced by a fall against a sharp corner. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned. sou-w Esma nooF Pmns,—J. S. Garland, Builders' Iron- monger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrhigton.—Advt.

rNORTHWICH SUBSIDENCE. The Local Board of Northwich have formally resolved to give Mr. Brunner, M.P., every assistance in the proiecution of his Subsidence Compensation Bill, which has been read a first time.

ALLEGED CRIMINAL ASSAULT. Al the Liverpool Assizes, on Thursday, John Lawrenson, 22, collier,, was found not guilty at Huyton, on the 27th July,crinlinally assaulted Mary Thresa Martindale against her will, and was dis- charged. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-4. IW. DIMON'S Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. AN ACTIVE WATCH COMMITTEE. The Watch Committee of the Liverpool .Corpora- don passed an important resolution, on Wednesday, in the form of a series of instructions to the Head ; Constable, to adopt rigorous measures for the sup- , pression of immoral houses, and to follow up the tenants with a view to preventing them from carry- ing on the same traffic elsewhere. PRESENTATION TO .A. WIDNES FOOTBALLER.

On. Wednesday evening a numerous company assembled in Anderson's Railway Hotel, Widnes, fcr the purpose of doing honour to Mr. J. E. Farrell, formerly, for many years captain of the Widnes Football Club. Dr. Richards presided, and Mr. Farrell was presented with a handsome marble clock and bronze ornaments. Afterwards a pleasant social evening was spent. SALT UNION BORING FOR OIL IN CHESHIRE. The Salt Union, believing that under the salt deposits of Cheshire are oil, gas, or coal, have com- menced boring operations at Olershaw-lane,Marston, Cheshire. The borings are not yet sufficiently deep to determine whether the union will be successful, but geologists have confidently assured the directors that under the salt beds natural ail or gas will certainly be found. The work is being prosecuted ' with the utmost Vigour.

WIDNES LOCAL• BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided and there were present Messrs. 1). Wright. B. Brown. J. Mid- wood, H. TimmiS, Geo. Neil, W. Hargreaves, R. Cook, F. Liddell, F. Heyes, J. Taylor. J. Houghton, S. Sadler, and Dr. O'Keeffe. with J. T. Allen, (clerk), S. Hoyle, (accou,ntant,;., I. Carr, (engineer), J. S. Sinclair, (surveyor), J.. Dickson, (inspector). MR. CAREY RESIGNS. The Clerk read the following letter from Mr. E. Carey: —" Dear Mr. Gosmge,l find that for some time to come I shall be so fully occupied with the work 1 have to do in connection with the United Alkali Company Limited, that I shall not be able to pay proper attention to my duties as a member of the Widnes Local Board. Under these circumstances I think it only right to place my resignation in your hands. I need hardly say it has been a very great pleasure to me to serve on the Board and I hereby offer you and ray colleagues my sincere thanks for the uniform kindness that has always been shown me. I shall always take a deep interest in Widnes and be only too glad to serve the interests of the town in any way in my power."—Dr. O'Keeffe said he regretted deeply that Mr. Carey should think fit to leave then) after being one of the most useful members of the Board fur a great number of years. (Hear. , hear.)—The Chairman: For 16 years.—Mr. Wright , seconded the motion. Mr. Carey, he said, had been a most valuable member of the Board, and it would be a pity to lose him after so many years faithful and valuable service to the town.—Mr. Brown supported the motion.—The Chairman said there . was no necessity for the letter to have been sent but Mr. Carey felt that be would be placing himself in a false position by not sending it, and he (the Chairman) thought the best plan would be to ask Mr. Carey to with- draw the letter. This suggestion was unanimously agreed to.

OVERDRAFTS. A lettet was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the auditors report on the overdrafts at the bank, and pointing out that there was no authority in law for large overdrafts to be created and they trusted that it' future the district rate .would be laid at such an amount in the £ for the year as would be suffi- cient to meet the year's current expenditure and thus terminate the present unsatisfactory state of affairs.— The Clerk explained that there were only three debit ac- counts in the treasurere account, and there were 10 or 11 other accounts. They were all treated as one account and the treasurer did not charge any interest for overdrafts. tithe Board would instruct him he could satisfactorily re- plf to ;this letter. It was stated at the weekly meeting at the West Derby Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, that the Garston Schools Committee had, in nonse- qnence of the strike, been compelled to grant school fees to 250 ektra familiea who had not previously applied for then. Fears were expressed that, im the event of the London and North-Western Rail-1 way Company persisting in their refusal to take any of the strike hands back, there would be heavy demands for relief owing to the men going off in search of work and leaving their families unpro- vided for.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. W. L. Pilkington, D.L., and Alderman Harrison, two members of the Ist Battalion Lancashire Regi- ment, named Charles Colman and Thomas Halligan, were charged with being absentees from their regi- ment, stationed at Warrington. They were arrested at a quarter to four that morning, and it transpired that.Veeirpastlee only permitted their absence up to 11-45 on Sunday night. The prisoners said they had been in the company of some friends, and missed the night train. They were at the station inquiring how soon they. could get to Warrington when they were arrested. If they CoUld hart; tea eh parade by a quarter to eight that morning nothing would have been said about their absence. They had re- relra tickets in their possession. The magis- trates discharged the• men, and advised them to get to Warrington as quickly as possible. USSDRELTAS RE-COVERED at the Shortest notlee.-3. & %W. DUTTON'S Sankey-fit.. Warrington.—Adrt.

- TUE QUESTION OF ALLOWING BAIL. At the Liverpool Assizes on Thursday, Patrick Gallagher, 19, collier, was indicted for having at Parr, on the 4th of October, criminally assaulted Ellen Murphy. He was acquitted at the conclusion of the case for the prosecution, the judge pointing out that there was no case. Having asked who had had the duty of getting up the prosecution, Mr. Justice Cave said it had been shockingly prepared, and greater care should be taken in these matters. In three cases that had been before him in this court the men had been acquitted, the evidence in each of them being of the slightest possible character yet the men had been kept in prison, some of them for a very Jong period. A little more care ought to be taken in ascertaining the facts in these cases, and when they were as slight as the three he had referred to, the men aught undoubtedly to be let out on bail. The following Is the copy of a letter which has been forwarded to the Vicar of St. Paul's in view of his removal to the living at Altrincham :—Warring- ton, December 11, 1890. Rev. Samuel Wilkinson, M.A. Dear sir.—l have much. pleasure in forward- ing you the enclosed resolution which was unani- mously passed at a special meeting of the Executive held on Tuesday last under the presidency of the Rev. John Yonge :—" Resolved that this Committee having learned w:th profound regret of the contem- plated. removal from Warrington, of the Rev. Samuel Wilkinson, M.A., the tirst President of this Federation, desires to place upon record its appre- ciation of his valuable labours in the cause of tem- perance in and around Warrington, and at the same time to express the fervent hope that he richest blesnngs of Almighty God will rest upon himself and Mrs. Wilkinson in their new home at Titnperley7'—l am, dear Mr. Wilkinson, yours faith- fully, Wm. 'Roberts, Hon. Secretary. üßurevw.As RE-COVERED at the shotteet notice.—J. & W. DUTTON 13 Serakey-et.. Warrington.—A"l. ST. FISLENS LIBERALS AND MR,. PARNELL.

The general committee of the S-ut-ton lAberal Club St. Helens, have unanimously passed the fol- lowing resolution and directed a copy to be for- warded to Mr. Gladstone :—" That, deploring Mr. Parnell's determination to retain the leadership of the Irish party, in spite of the enlightened sudg- ment cf the English nation, and ,of the best minds of his own party, as likely to do incalculable rats- chief to the cause of Ireland and to involve the re- tirement of Mr. Gladstone, this meeting desires to expressits sympathy with and unwavering trust in Mr. Gladstone, and hopes that he may be able to re- main leader of a united and victorious Liberal party."' At a meeting of the St. Helens branch of the Na- tional League, on Sunday, the question of the Par- nell crisis was discussed, and ultimately a rescilu-, tion was unanimously passed, that that 'branch of the League was entirely in sympathy with the: majority of the Dish Parliamentary representatives, and that Mr. Parnell should retire from the leader- ship of the party, and the secretary Was instructed to telegraph the resolution to Mr. Justin McCarthy,' M.?.—At a meeting of the executive of the Helens Liberal Association, on Tuesday evening, the following resolution was unanimously -adopted: —" This Executive Committee unanimously desires to express its unabated conhdence in the leadership of Mr. Gladstone, and places upon record its loyalty to him in his policy of Home Rule, and renews its pledge to use every effort to return Mr. W. IL Ken- nedy, Q.C., at the next election as a supporter of justice to Ireland."

Brookes, representing the Police- men's and Tradesmen's Cricket Clubs, attended the meeting for the purpose of formally handing over a horse ambulance and two hand ambulances or the use of the Accident Hospital.—Superintendent Noblett who was the spokesman of the party, said these appliances, as was well-known were much required in Widnes where there were very large works in which accidents frequently happened, and last summer the two cricket clubs repre- sented, played a match for the purpose of raising a fund to purchase the ambulances, and also collected subscrip- tions with the same object. The people of Widnes liberally responded and the ambulances were now in front of the Town Hall awaiting the inspection of the Board, and he had great pleasure in handing them over to the custodyof the Board fully paid for.—The members then went and examined the ambulances and on return- ing expressed their sense of their character and usofulness. —The Chairman proposed that they be thankfully accepted by the Board and that the cordial thanks of the members be accorded to the donors. Mr. Brown seconded the motion which was.then carried and the deputation withdrew. riIIEVENTION OF INFECTIOUS orsussas. Mr. D. Wright moved that the Infectious Diseases Prevention Act, 1890, be adopted by the !Soard and come into operation within the district on the 16th January next. There had been, Mr. Wright said, a difficulty in getting people to go to the hospital, and it had also been found that in some instances bodies had been taken ' from the hospital to the houses of relatives or friends of the deceased, a custom which had led to the spread of infectious disease. In the interests of the health of the peppletit was the duty of the Board to adopt the Act. Mr. Timmins seconded the motion which was carried with- mit discussion.
TUE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.

FOUR WARDS OR SIX WARDS. This subject came before Widnes Local Board, at their meeting an Tuesday, on a recommendation from the General Purposes Committee. The Com- mittee had examined and considered ten different schemes for dividing the town into wards, and advised the Board to adopt No. 8, with four wards. —Mr. Wright proposed the acceptance of this re- commendation.—Dc. O'Keeffe coaoved an amendment that No. 4 scheme, by which the town was divided into six wards, be adopted. He contended that public opinion was in favour of six wards, and said they might as well remain a Local Board as only have four wards, because that would only give them one more member than they had at present; and men who had an ambition to serve the town would not have a chance of becoming members of the Cor- poration. There was an immense amount of latent talent buried in the town which ought to be utilized. He also argued that were No. 8 scheme adopted a redistribution of seats would have to take place in a few years at a great cost to the ratepayers, and they had far better take the bull by the horns at once and adopt what the vast majority, of the electors of Widnes wished for.—Mr. Hargreaves seconded the motion because he considered No. 4 Scheme decidedly the best.—Mr. Hayes said his great objection to No. 4 was that itplaced one third of the representation on West Bank.—Mr. O'Keefe said the population of West Bank was certain to decrease in a short time.—Mr. Fleyes : And the representatives would not be taken away.—Mr. Taylor was in favour of No. B.—The Chair- ran said it did not wafter whether they decided on a schema that day or not, and something bad come to his knowledge which he was not at librety to make public which would have an important bearing upon the sub- ject. He suggested that the matter should be discussed in committee and fully threshed out before next meeting without any delay being caused in the application for the Charter of Incorparation.—The members unanim- ously agreed to this course. No. 8 plan contained four wards, and the first ward which contained 882 burgesses, is bounded on two sides by Cronton and Bold, and on the others by Steward's footpath, Deacon-road and Halton View. The second ward .eontains 1,285 burgesses and is bounded by the St. Helens (Anal Lugsdale-road, Widnes-road, Albert-road, and Halton- view. The third ward contains 1,136 burgesses, and the boundary is Stewards-lane footpath to Deacon-road, Widnes-road, Lugsdale-road, i.onn-5t., and the London and North-Western Railway. The fourth ward contains 1,519 .bergesses, and includes the whole of the West Bank, the boundary being. the London and North-Wes- tern Railway line to St. Helens canal. The No. 4 plan contains six wards, the first being bounded by Cronton and Bold, Stewards footpath, Deacon-road, Peelhouse- lane, and Cheshire Lines Railway, and contains 551 bur- gesses. The second ward has 774 burgesses. and is bounded by the St. Helens canal, St. Helens Railway, Peelhouse-lane, Cheshire Lines Railway, and Cuerdley. No, 3 ward 957 burigesses; bounded by stewards foot.

path, Deacon-rd.,Albert-rd., St. Helens Railway,Gerrard- st., Milton-road, and Ditton Township. No. 4 ward 1,001 burgesses, bounded by Ditton, Milton-road, Gerrard-st., St. Helens Railway, and London and North-Western Railway. No. 5 ward 1,010 burgesses, bounded by the London and North-Western Railway Viaduct, St. Helens Railway, and river Mersey. div.head: RUNCORN RIFLE VOLUNTEERS
div.p: RUNCORN RIFLE VOLUNTEERS

DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. , The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connection with-the Runcorn detachment of the 2nd (Earl of Chester's) V.B. Cheshire Regiment took place on Honda) evening in Runcorn Public Hall. Theteserved seats were occupied by a fashionable company, and there was a fair attendance of the general public in other parts of the Hall. Mr. John Brun- drit J.P., presided, and he was supported on the plat- form by Colonel Ashton, Major Flintt, Major Hazlehurst, Major Jolliffe, Captain Wigg, and Mrs. Henry Reynolds, of Frodsham, who had kindly consented to distribute the prizes. During an interval lathe pragramme, the Chair- man delivered a speech in which he expressed the plea- sure he felt at presiding on that occasion, which had a peculiar interest to him in many ways. Although it was a long time since he was a volunteer, he could not forget that on the following day it would be exactly 31 years ago that he was enrolled one of the first members of that corps. (Applause) That was a long while to look back upon, and many who were now in the ranks were not born in that day, but still long as it was his feelings of interest and affection for the service had not abated in any way, and he believed the volunteers would prove thsmselves equal to all emergencies if ever called upon to exercise their powers. (Applause.) He did not wish to enter into a dissertation on foreign wars. We knew what our soldiers had proved themselves capable of accomplishing when occasion required, and he did not hesitate to say that the Volunteers would show at home that British pluck which their brethren had displayed on battle fields afar. (Applause.) The Chairman then introduced Mrs. Rey- nelds to carry out the part of the programme allotted to her, and described her as a member of a family long resident in the neighbourhood, and highly honouredand.. esteemed.— (Applause.) Mrs. Reynolds then distributed the prizes to the suc- cessful Volunteers, who all appeared in uniform. Afterwards Captain Wigg proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Reynolds for her kindness, and the motion being seconded by Major Flintt; was carried by acclamation. —Mrs. Reynolds appropriatsly acknowledged the vote. Colonel Ashton proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man, and remarked that had Mr. Brundrit not retired from the corps he would now have been the Colonel of the Regiment (applause) and he (Col. Ashton) felt nat- tered to think he would have had a regiment he need not have been ashamed of. (Applause.) At the present time they were not quite up to their full strength; the maximum was 906, and they were at the present time 822. He was sorry to Fay there were 18 who were not efficient, but they would agree with him that was not a large auct Yrlm ttAt Pt V•ii,se wcrs chaplains (Inghter) it Spolte very well for the fighting force.—Major Jolliffe seconded the pro- posal which was heartily carried.—The Chairman having responded, the entertainment was proceeded with. The entire programme was sustained by Mr. Harold Whalley, of Liverpool, who gave a highly clever and amusing entertainment consisting ef character sketches inter- spersed with appropriate songs. Ills various "hits" at "Society" were highly diverting. In the course of the evening, the brass band of the corps, performed several selections in capital style. DETACHMENT NIUE% Prizes.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUN-
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUN-
CORN.

The last of the series of lectures on political • economy was given by Mr. Llewllyn Smith, 8.A., in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday. There was only a moderate attendance. The subject for the evening was Trades Unionism, and the Lecturer said any independent observer who was asked to name a salient feature of the social life of England in the last few years,would say that it was the rise ot combinations and of associated efforts of all kinds not necessarily industrial. We found that industry tended more and more to fall into the hands of joint stock com- binations on one side, and on the other side, was the la- bourer, and the present century had seen the rise of the two great sets of workmens' combinations, trades unions and co-operative societies. This tendency to manage things by associated efforts was characteristic of an advanced stage of civilization ; they did not find it amongst many of the races of mankind ;it required in addition to self-government, the power to subordinate the individual to the community,and to forego immediate gain in prospect of future advantage. All these qualities, which were rare qualities, were necessary for successful combined action. In conclusion Mr. Smith dealt with productive co-opera- tion, which he described as an attempt at democracy in industry.—The Rev. Canon Wood proposed a vote of ' thanks to Mr. Smith for the series of lectures he had given. They owed him their cordial thanks for the way iTi which he bad fought against the difficulties of the course, and for affording them many subjects for thought. Mr. Smith was the assistant secretary of a Technical Education Association in London, and he had given the Runcorn Committee very healthful suggestions to cheer and eneourag,e them in doing what they could. Mr. E. Marshall seconded the motion, remarking that in an industrial centre like Runcorn, it was important that they should be well founded in the principles of political enconomy, and no one could have listened to Mr. Smith's lectures without being greatly helped in understanding the many problems which were agitating the public mind. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried by accla- mation, and Mr. Smith, in reply, said he did not think numbers an essential in lectures of this kind. If a few got an increased interest in social and economic ques- tions, that seemed to him to be the main thing to be hoped from a course of extension lectures.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys announced that the next coMse would be commenced on Friday, January 9th. The sub- ject is "The Making of Nations," and Mr. H. J. Mac- Kinder will be the lecturer.
