div.head: , LOCAL LIBEL • ACTION.
div.p: , LOCAL LIBEL • ACTION.
TRIAL YRSTRRDAY.-IIEAVY DAAIAGESI

------- - - - Yesterday, at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Wills, and a special jury, Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth, solicitors, Warrington, brought an action against John Warburton, farmer, near War- rington, to recover damages for an alleged libel. Mr. Gully, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Pickford (instructed by Mr. Spencer Wellhead) appeared for the plain- tiffs, and Mr. Bigham and Mr. Horridge (instructed by Messrs. Waring Cropper and Co., Liverpool) ap- peared for the defendant. Damages were also claimed from Thomas Fuller, Liverpool, the printer , of the alle:ed libel, for whom Mr. Addison, Q.C., ' , .M.P., and Mr. Horridge appeared. Mr. Gully explained the facts of the case to the jury. He pointed out that Mrs. Warburton engaged the plaintiffs to act for her in some legal proceed- ings, having for their object the obtaining of a judicial separation from her husband, and that in consequence of the steps taken by the plaintiffs, the defendant Warburton published a series of cir- culars, insulted Mr. Jenkins in public, andin other ways annoyed him. The first of the libellous cir- culars described Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth as bully lawyers. and stated that they had just added to their -business the most improved system of separating husbands from wives, and wives from husbands, and earnestly soliciting patronage. A second circular was to the same effect, but with an addition suggesting that the office was opened " in the small hours of the morning when the cats go rambling and howling " for immoral purposes, and a further circular contained statements to the same effect. Mr. Gully said the suggestion was as utterly unfounded as it was gross. Mr. IV. H. J. Jenkins, one of the plaintiffs, said in May last year he was consulted by the wife of War- burton, with regard to obtaining a judicial separa- tion. A petition was put in, and a few days after- wards he met Warburton at Padgate, and he tried to drive over him. Witness had to get into the ditch out of the way. Warburton also used foul and in- sulting language. He afterwards received a letter of apology from the defendant. Shortly before the petition came on for hearing, a reconciliation was effected between Warburton and his wife, and the petition was withdrawn, an agreement being drawn , up in which defendant agreed to pay debts, costs of ' the action, settle a life policy on his wife and children, and the farm to be carried on by the wife. In August, this year, he was again instructed to take proceedings for a judicial separation. Soon after this, on the 20th August, he saw a circular, which was in the handwriting of the defendant Warburton. A week afterwards he received another similar circular, and behind was stamped " Jen- keens, Maidstone and Unswater, bully lawyers Hocsemarket-st.,. Warrington." On the third Sep- tember he got a further circular, and on the 10th a further hatch. Hundreds had been circulated. On the 22nd September it became necessary to take possession of Callun's farm. This was carried out, and the next day he received from the defendant's son, William, a great number of circulars found at the farm which had not been sent out. The circu- lars continued to be seat out after the action was commenced. He received the stamp by which the circulars were stamped from Mrs. Warburton. The defendant had also annoyed witness in various -ways. Cross-examined by Mr. Bigham : The writ in -tlie action was issued on the 10th Septembr, and the last circular on the I.3th. The issue of the cir- culars did not cease with the issue of the writ. When defendant had met witness be had said "Here comes Brierlev," referring to the Brierley who -figured in the Maybrick case. Mr. Bighata expressed the opinion that the , libels were very offensive, and he understood the action was brought to prevent their continu- ance. ' Mr. Gully said the Object was to give the defend- ant such a lesson as to teach him 'setter than libel a respectable tirmof solicitors. Mr. Bight= naked if the witness believed that ' the circulars had been taken seriously by anyone in 1 Warringt on. :.s. Witness said it had affected him seriously. Mr. Gully: Has it affected your business. Witness: Mere particularly in health. Mr. Cully produced a song called "Driven from Home," published I,y the defendant. The song on the title page was stated to be by "William Henry Jenkins, alias Brierley, a facsimile of the man wbo 'figured soprominetstly in the Maybrick case. The IWoras of the song were read out to the jury. Mr. Bigharn asked witness what we% the condi- tion of the defendant's mind 11 , • Witness: Very wicked. Mr. Bi2ham: Is it weak I' Witness: .Not when his interests have to be studied. Mr. Bigharn : Have you said that his family ought to lock him up inn lunatic asyluna? Witness: I have said I hoped they would. I should be very thankful if his friends would place ' him in an asylum. Mr. Qully, referring' to the song, said the defend- ant described himself as shoeless, shelSerless, &c. Was the defendant poor? , Witness: No, he came in for .£5,000 the other day under his mother's will. Mr. Unsworth, the other plaintiff, also gave en- deuce, and said Warburton had insulted him in public'. ' William Warburton, the son of the defendant, also gave evidence. Cross-examined by Mr. Bighorn, the witness said his father Was eccentric, and asked how lie showed it, he said he wore a, black.hat. .

Mr. Bigham said he should be characterised as eccentric if that was the evidence. (Laughter.) Witness said this was a very black hat. His father had also gone about with his coat turned in- side out. He believed he had been in a lunatic asylum some 15 or 16 years ago. This concluded the plai,:tiff's case. The defence intimated that they ,did not purpose calling any evidence, and Mr. Gully, for the plaintiffs, summed up and com- mented at some length on the evidence. , Mr. Bikham, replying on behalf of the .defendant Warburton, admitted that all the things done by . Mr. Jenkins on behalf of Mrs. Warburton were ' properly done, but they were things which would irritate a man, and which he hoped would prove some sort of an excuse for defendant's conduct. ' With regard to the question of damages, he, on be- half of the defendant, expressed his deep regret that he had ever been led into publishing these circulars. _ _ _

His lordship, addressing the jury, said he thought the libel bad been brought home to the defendants, and reasonable and competent damages ought to be given. The defendants were very fortunate indeed that they were not at the other end of the build- ing instead of at that end. He thought if they had been they would have met with much more un- pleasant circumstahces than any which might follow their verdict. _
The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiffs, and assessed the damages at £250 against Warburton and £5O against Fuller, for which judgment was given. _
A second case brought by Mr. Jenkins personally against Warburton, was settled by the defendant paying .£2O and the costs.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ATTEMPTING TO RESCUE A PRISONER.

At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday, a soldier 'named, Thomas Moore, was charged with attempting to rescue a prisoner from the custody of the police, and assaulting Police-constable Faulkner in Buttermarket-st., the previous night. The evidence showed that several constables had a man named Benson in custody on a charge of drunk and disorderly, when Moore came up and endeavoured to drag him away. Ile also struck Police-constable Faulkner a violent blow on the mouth. —Sergeant Craythorne, from Orford Barracks, gave pri- soner a bad character. A fine of £5 and costs was imposed, or in default two months imprisonment with hard labour.
SHOCKING ASSAULT CASE.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Friday. Annie MiMe was summoned for assaulting Maria Alice Jones.— Complainant said defendant went to her house 20, Cros- fteld-st., on Saturday night and asked if her (defendant's) husband was there. Complainant answered that he was not, and told defendant if she choosed she could walk in and see for herself. Defendant then began to make a bother and struck witness on the face with a satchel, causing a black eye When a policeman appeared on the scene she (complainant) was bleeding on the face.—Mr. Jones said defendant's husband had worked for him. The woman had been a drunnrd for a number of years and was well known to the police at Liverpool. De- fendant's husband had at one time had £6,500, but It was lost, and he had also lost. several situations all through her.' Ultimately the defendant was bound over, on her own surety of £lO to keep the peace towards corn- p'aMant for six months. PECULIAR AND Scnious THEFT.

A young woman named Annie McCann, was arrested upon a warrant in Ireland, on Monday, by Detective- Sergeant Monaghan. and brought before the magistrates sitting at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with stealing a box, containing a quantity of clothing to the value of £2O, from the Cheshire Lines Railway, at Warrington Station. Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted on behalf of the Company and said the case was not only a serious one, but was also a peculiar one. On the Bth Nov. prisoner came to Warrington from Stockport and asked a porter (Buckley) to put two boxes which she claimed as hers on the cab. On the 10th ult , prisoner returned to the station, and complained of hav- ing lost a box. The railway officials made full enquiries Ica the box; but could not trace of it. an the meantime a claim of £2O was made against the Company by, Miss Holland, of Southport, for the loss of a box consigiied to her from Stockport. On Wednesday, prisoner and her master went to the station and the latter handed to the official Miss Holland's box properly addressed. Prisoner went to Southport, saw Miss Holland, and told her that she had taken her box in mistake for the one which she said she had lost. Miss Holland believed her story and gave prisoner a letter which was afterwards flaunted before the railway officials. Prisoner then admitted that she had lost no box, and treated the matter humorously. The railway officials, however, took an entirely different view of the case in consideration of the trouble they had been put to, and when they found that Miss Holland's box had, been broken open, although nothing had been takes out, they took cut a warrant for prisoner's arrest. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for two months.

WIDNES Aseutt..—These teams- met at VVidnes bPfore a good attendance. The game opened evenly, when the homesters forced a minorpoint.. Dropping out the Widnesians had the better-of matters, but could not score. At the interval no. tangible points had been scored. The second half was as hotly contested as the first portion, and as nothing was scored, the game re- sulted in a draw of 1 minor to nil.

SALE V. RUNCORN.—PIayed at Sale. Runcorn were short of seven of the usual team. The hornesters made a good start, Stephens scoring and Cookson placed the goal. The visitors fairly roused thernselbee after this reverse, and up to the interval crossed the home line four times, Davies, Pendlebury, Sampson,. and Evans, being the scorers. Turning round, the Runcornians kept up the attack, and 'lampoon and Wood in turn scored and May dropped a goal, Harvey obtaining an, unimproved try for the home side. Result—Runcorn sgoals and 4 tries ; Sale, 1 goal and 1 ti-v. WARRINGTON " A." V. Tuxotst.nr "w."—Owing to a late arrival, this match which was played at Tyldesley, was limited to two twenties. Tyldesley started the game against a slight breeze, but a free kick early on resulted in Jolley gaining a considerable advantage by a huge punt. This was to some extent neutralized by a strong rush, headed by Sampson, Shepherd, and' Stnith, until Knowles, Dawes, Barnes, and Russell carried the oval well into their opponents' lines. A lot of light pack work ensued near the Warrington lines, the homesters having the best of the argument in the scrums, but, at length, the danger was averted, mainly through the grand tackling powers of Davies. Again Tyldeslev swept down, but Boscow got the ball away beadifnlly. Then followed some very effective play by Rowe and Jolley, and the position was further enhanced by some capital following up by Isherwood, Russell, and Barnes. The homesters, who were playing a strong game,again came away, Sampson saving finally at midfield, and punting back to the home lines. Following this,.a terrific kick by Jolley rolled dead. Succeeding the drop out,] Creagitan, Molyneaux,;Teare, and Lally headed a com- bined dribble, Tyldesley for some time being hard pressed, which ended in Daniels running over finely front a quick low pass by Rowe. Isherwood improved the point by a grand kick fronatouch. Re-starting, Fearnley,Worthing- ton, and Hampson rushed down the field,but Bbsccrw was all there, and chiefly by the instrumentality of Povey, Davies, Molyneux, and Knowles, the ball was taken beyond the centre line. Jolley- then ran grandly, and screwing across Teare got a well-earned try under the posts, the place failing. Fluctuating play followed, Shepherd, by a powerful run, eventually taking the leather to midfield. From here the game was taken to the Warrington lines, and after a scramble.. Worthing- ton scored, half-time arriving with Warrington 1-1-1, to 0-1-0. Resuming, the ball was soon in the home 25, some Pretty passing between Rowe. Lally, and Jolley getting the sphere near the lines. Lally's smartness was at this period very noticeable, as were a couple of grand pieces of work by Daniels. div.head: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.

ATTEMITED SUICIDE.—At this Court. on Friday morn- ing, Michael Hamilton, aged 25, a collier, living at New Boston,Haydock. was charged with attempting to com- mit suicide on the 2nd inst.. It appeared that the Sunday previous to this date prisoner jumped through the window at his house, and on the day in question he jumped into the resevoir at Queen pit, the water at the time being eight feet deep. He sank twice and was then rescued by a brakesman in the employ of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Defendant was brought before the magistrates the following day, and remanded to the workhouse, and on Friday he was discharged.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY.

Warrington were voted unlucky on Saturday, in not being able to register a victory over Tyldesley. For 58 ' out of the 80 minutes played, the Warringtonians were leading by three tries, all the result of brilliant exhibi- tions, and it was only in the last two minutes of the game that the Tyldesley men, taking advantage of the scrambling nature of the play, succeeded in scoring a try from which a pal was kicked, thus equalizing the points gained by Warrington. Massey and Frank Turner made their re-appearance in the team after a lengthened absence. There would be three thousand present when Shaw kicked off towards the pavilion goal. play at the opening being generally Confined to the half-way. A clever run by Fearnley, and a screw kick by Shaw took play direct to the Warrington line. Webster ran the oval out, and Berry came away from the ruck, only tp find Gibbods cleverly respon ding, and Warrington had all their work cut out to prevent the visitors from scor- ing. The homesters had not apparently settled down to their work, but eventually a fine forward movement, headed by Jolley, Holmes, and Ashton, was spoiled by over eagerness, and Fair Turner having a kick charged, Evans luckily cleared. Bate and Barnes passed neatly, and the former again securing, Tyldesley now set up a defence against the persistent attack of the Warring- tonians. Some transfers between Bate, Barnes, and Massey gained but little ground, the tackling being safe. Gibbons and Frank Turner exchanged kicas, but still the " Bongers " could not clear. Bate cleverly eluded Hanson and then a grand spell of passing between Fair Turner, Barnes, and Webster, found the latter being pulled up a yard from the line. Several palpable chances of scoring were missed by Warrington, and play was still confined to the Tyldesley line. A grand run by Bate raised the enthusiasm, and Shaw and Barnes exchanging kicks, the former punted to Fearnley, but Ashton's height serving him to advantage, the reply was charged, and a bold and successful bid was made for a try. Fair Turner took the place, which was opposite the corner flag, and a splendid attempt was made, the ball hitting the crossbar, and rebounding into play. Hostilities were carried on at the visiting 25, and Jolley with a grand dribble almost notched a try. Barnes let slip a rare chance, and a spell of passing along the line deserved a better fate. However, from a scrim- mage, Bate tried to force an vening, but without success, and Jolley next secured possession, and after a strong run crossed the line, Fair Turner making another good bid for the major point. Dillon, Bandies, and Thorniley shone with sterling work after the drop out, and a long pass from Mather to Barnes was productive of the only minor in the match. Bate. Massey, and Barnes again passed, but nothing resulted, and half time was called as Warrington 0-2-1, Pyldesley nil. Directly on resuming, Massey almost got in from a pass by Barnes. The latter, however, astonished the spectators a moment later, for securing possession from Bate at half-way, he ran and dodged in his own inimitable style, and a brilliant run ended in his scoring a try, although he almost came to grief a yard from the line, when he slipped. The kick at goal was again at fault. Darkness was fast coming on, and it was a hard task to distin- guish individual play on the popular side. Jolley shone with a useful dribble, but Fearnley with a judicious kick gave his side a footing in the home quarters. A bout of: passing by the Tyldesley backs was frustrated by Webster, but still the Warringtonians defended. Ashton, Berry. and Frank Turner essayed to clear with a fruit- less result, and Tyldesley, taking advantage of the apparent timidity of the home backs, kept up the pres- sure. Bate made his mark under difficulties. A run by Fair Turner, dribbling by Jolley, and passing by Bates, Barnes, and Massey all tended to relieve, but the effort was only momentary, for some scrambling play ensued in the Warrington quarters' and J. Fearnley ultimately scored, Shaw placing a goal and Tyldesley luckily malt- ing a draw, the final score reading—Warrington, 0-3-1 ; Tyldesley, 1-0-0. Teams :—Warrington : J. W. Evans, back ; J. T. Massey (captain), T. Barnes, and 11. Webster three-quarter-backs ; James Bates, and S. Mather, half- backs ; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, E. Dillon, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, J. T. Thorniley, H. Holmes, and W. Berry, forwards. Tyldesley; I. Gibbons, back ; J. Fearnley (captain), F. Shaw, and I. Clarke, three- quarter backs ; W. Berry and W. Hanson, half-backs G. Woodward, p. Battersby, W. Sutcliffe, A. Smith, A. Foy, P. Fearnley, G. Mercer, J. Forbes, T. Hilton, for- wards. Referee, Mr. S. Simpson (Broughton Rangers).

Nl—der why-on earth the catastrophe came to pass. The Council has hitherto Adjusted the annual County Cricket Tournament very satisfactorily. The only difficulty was a difficulty in prospect, arising out of the scheme of classification which was adopted in! August, and which pressed rather unfairly on the second-class counties. This difficulty, which the War- wickshire proposal would have got over, in a fashion, certainly does not look insoluble. After discussing it, however, for an hour or two, the Council could find nothing better to do than to vote itself out of existence. Perhaps Mr. Webbe—the Parnell of the situation—will now explain what he has to propose next.

WARRINGTON V. BIRKENHEAD:,

This match was played at Arpley on Saturday. Warrington were short of four of their best men. The• centres faced at 2.45, and the play at once became fast and even, both goals being visited in turn, And for some time Warrington having the best of the game. The visi- tors now attacked, but could not put the rubber past. Barker. R. E. Garnett threw up the field, and the home attacks kept the visitors' defence busy,..but C. Tilley re- lieved by throwing down. After about twenty minutes even play, A. H. Tilley secured, and running down the wing passed to Stott, who scored. The game now cOn- tinned even, Gossage, Graves, and A. Cruttended put in some work. The home team were then hard pressed. ' exciting scrimmages occurring in the goal mouth. R. Garnett gave relief, and the Warrington attacks gave Birkenhead defence some trouble. Gessage and Wall placed the home goal in • danger, but Barker saved mira- culously. Wall getting possesion transferred to Stott, who scored again. The Warringtonians now warmed to their work. R. E. Garnett cleared with a long shy to Jones, who shot at goal, but Clibborn saved, and Smith following up put the ball, through the posts, and at the interval Birkenhead led by two goals to one. During the second half, which lasted only twenty minutes, the Warrington men fell off. On the'other hand, Birkenhead played a much better game, and their attacks ' were almost irrestible. Kiernan and R. Garnet strove hard to stop the visitors scoring, but Stott added two goals, .and Wall shortly afterwards scored the Afth and last for his side, and Birkenhead retired winners of a well con- tested and pleasant game by five goals to one. The visi- tors' defence all held their men, while Gossage, Wall, and Stott were the pick of the attack. For Warrington Barker in goal was a treat to watch; he stopped some splendid shots, and cleared in beautiful style, he being ably assisted by R. Garnett, Kiernan, and R. E. Garnett, whilst on the attack Smith and Jones were most promin- ent. Teams :—Birkenhead: R. B. Clibborn, C: G. Tilley, A. H. Groves, P. B. Cruttenden, A. H. Tilley, .3.. P. Rudolf, C. Wall, A. Stott, J. Crooks, R. H. Gossage, C. Graves.and A.G. Cruttenden. Warrington: H. Barker, R. Gamett,'W. A. Kiernan, R. E. Garnett, E. Warburton, R. Henry, C. E. Bennett, 11. Smith, H. S. Jones, L. Thompson, C. Spinks, and H. Tetlow.
THE ATTEMPT TO IROWN A WOMAN AT WARRINGTON. VERDICT AT THE ASSIZES.

At the Liverpool Assizes. on Wednesday,. Thomas Hall (50), puddler, was indicted for having at War— rington, on the 29th Septgmbertattemptedito drown Mary Lyons, with intent to murder. Mr..Shee pro- secuted, and Mr. Segar defended. The evidence showed that on the date mentioned the prisoner prisoner and the woman were on the banks of the Mersey at Poulton, Warrington, when a quarrel arose with reference to some money. The prisoner was heard saying, "If you don't give me the money back, I will throw you into the river,'" A struggle occurred between them, the result being that the prisoner pushed her into the water. The woman sank twice, and was only rescued with difficulty by two men, who came up. When the woman was conveyed to the police-station she- was very ex- hausted and sick, and vomited some black din i y water. When charged the prisoner replied, " I did it in the heat of passion. She robbed me. I would , not have hurt Catherine for the world."—Mr. Seger contended: that there was no intent on the part of the prisoner to murder the woman. The dispute arose out of a paltry matter, and was not in any way likely to lead to murderous results. The prisoner had probably no knowledge of the depth of the water and when he found the prosecutrix was in the river he handed her Ins belt, in order to help to get her out.—The jury found the prisoner not guilty, and he was discharged.

ASSIZES,.

Two Polish seamen,. mined Domanaki, Dovitsk and Josephiftemakis, were put upon theirttialion Monday at the Liverpool Assizes,for unlawfully wounding Sylvester Onstrao on the 25th August at Widnes_ A verdict of "Nat guilty" was returned', and the, prisoner was dis- charged: _

Tli'omeus O'Neil' (29),. labourer,. {Widnes, pleaded not guilty-to an indictment charging him with unlawfully wounchug his son- Ames (6), with intent to do him grevious bodily harm. The,prisoner„who, had thrashed his child with the buckle end of al belt„ was sentenced to four months imprisonment with hard labour. John Mullarkey (41), baker, Widnes was indicted, for having on the Nt November unla,wfUlliwounded Charles Mclbughlin with, intent to do, him grievous bodily harm. —Mr.- Formby, who. prosecuted, stated, that on the 25th October prosecutor befriended the-prisoner, giving him and his family a shelter, while prisoner looked for work. Prosecutor's hoese being a 'small one, the family of the prosecutor were- very much incommoded. Accordingly, on theist. Noreinber„ prosecutor told prisoner he could not let him stay there any longer_ This seemed to have annoyed the prisoner, who, after brooding over the mat- terrall day, asked prosecutor in the evening if he could remain at hishouse. Prosecutor said he could not, as the place WAS too small. Thereupon, prisoner said, ;‘LWell;.Charley„l'll stab you, and then kill myself "* • • and drawing, a knife from his pocket, he opened it, and - made a blow at prosecutor's chest. Prosecutor warded the blow off with his hand, receiving a severe cut on th . wrist. Prisoner then threw himself on the door, and. pretended to stab himself, but only cut his coat.—Dr.. Hutchinson stated that he had great difficulty in sto ping the bleeding of the wound. It was doubtfu , whether hevrould recover the use of his hand.—The jurttN found the prisoner guilty, and his Lordship, in passing- ' sentence, said that the prisoner had exhibited base gratitude. The prosecutor had taken him in when he was without a borne, and given him a share of his moue for a week. Because prosecutor could give him that shelter no lOnger, prisoner deliberately took out a klisfe and attempted to stab him in the chest. Prisoner would have to go into penal servitude for five years. Michael Donlan, 37, labourer, was arraigned em a charge of having unlawfully wonnded Myles Damn, on the 16th of Angust.—The case for the prosecution, was that the parties are labourers, and worked at the Widnes Alkali Works, and on the 16th of August prosecutor went to the Crown Vaults, Ann-street West, Widnes. Prisoner was there at the time, and asked the complainant to stand him a drink. Darcy declined to do so, arid! some words ensued between the parties. Prisoner eventually picked up a glass which was half full of beer, rsendlhing it with great violence at Darcy. The glass caught Darcy on the right_cheek, and the complainant was knocked down, and was rendered unconscious. On being;chazged prisoner replied " I don't know anything about It; I was drunk."—For tbe defence the theory was,setup that complainant,who was alleged to have beendrimitjed on to the broken glass, and thus sustained his injUries.—The jury returned a verdict of guilty of unlawfab wounding against the prisoner, and it was stated by the.polfice that he was previously a man of good character,, and was very quiet, but was very passionate when, drtenk.—ln consequence of the good character givens,. his. Lordship only sentenced the prisoner to four monthehard labour. Benjamin Davies (31),Iabourer' was put upon his trial, on a charge of unlawfully and maliciously wounding Michael Brennan, at Widnes, on the 23UL October, with ' intent to do him grievous bodily harm._ The case for the prosecution was that the parties were-drinking together in the public-house, and afterwards went together to tho prisoner's house. There a. quarrel took place. Prosecu- tor attempted to leave the house' but before he could reach the door he was struck with something hard by the prisoner, the blow causing him to fall to the ground: On being picked up it was found that he had received a. serious wound on the side of the head, which for a tcoe placed him in danger. When apprehended on the follwov- ing morning prisoner produced the mouthniece oD a. musical instrument, saying "That is what I did it with." P.S. McGregor said that from inquiries he had mad e• he found that prisoner had lived for 25 years in Widnes,and had had the character of being a hard-working respect- ' able man.—The jury found prisoner guilty of unlawfully wrunding.—His Lordship in consideration of the good character which had been given the prisoner, by the police-sergeant, nar.ed a sentence of pnly six, weeks' imprisonment with hard labour.

wish to correct a mistake in my letter last week. It should have read —the question was never discussed until the Novomber township meeting.—Yours &e., E. CROSS.
Penketh, Dec. llth, 1890.
THE MEMORIAL SERMON.

Sir,—On Sunday evening last, the writer listened to an excellent sermon at Wycliffe Chapel in memory of the late Mr. Rigby. lam led to believe that among the con- gregation were several who have not the pleasure of be- longing to Wycliffe, but who had come out of respect to the memory of the deceased gentleman. Under these circumstances, I would, with all courtesy, suggest that the rather sneering references to the Church of England might for once have been omitted—Yours faithfully, B. Warrington, Dec. 10th, 1890..

It sicdpiy pains one to Mee youths lounging round bars and 'billiard tablt..2 'with cigarette or pipe between their lips, when they might, and I think ought to be at the feet of the teachers of subjects that would be useful, and are,in- deed, highly essential to their future welfare, morally., physically, and pecuniarily. By inserting these few lines together with the enclosed in your next impression you will oblige yours truly, THOMAS MORRIS.
December 10, 1890. [ENCLOSURE.] THE EMPLOYMENT OF FOREIGN CLERKS.

Thd Lord Mayor has directed the following letter to be forwarded to the secretary of of the ,City Clerks' Alli- ance, in reply to a communication calling upon him to use his influence with the City business firms to induce them to discontinue the practice of employing so many German and other foreign clerks while thousands of English clerks are out of etnoloyment : The Mansion House London- December 2.

• Dear Sir,—The Lord. Mayor is sorry that he cannot in- tervene or assist in the matter about which you write. He much regrets to hear that there are so many English clerks out of employment, but masters have a right to choose their own employes, and if they find they get better served by foreign clerks, either from a linguistic or other point of view, he cannot see what is to prevent them obtaining that service. Still, he would always hope that, qualifications being equal, English clerks would receive a preference over foreigners.—Yours, etc., W. SOULSBY.

MR. PEERS AND "IMPERFECT REPORTING." Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last, I notice that Mr. Peers refers to me, in a respectful and friendly manner, as having read a paper on "Common-sense versus Critic- ism "at a meeting of the "Wycliffe Young People's Society." So far he is quite correct, and within the limit of fact; but in a most extraordinary fashion he proceeds to draw upon his imagination and to fall foul upon what he calls " imperfect reporting." I cannot but' marvel how ever he allowed his letter to lease his hands without discovering his much more faulty and " imperfect " reasoning. "Imperfect reporting " may sometimes be excused, imperfect reasoning never.

It appears that Mr. John Gandy had read a paper on Count Tolstoi at the Penketh Mutual Improvement Asso- ciation, and that the " gist " of the paper had been entirely neglected in the report. Not being present my- self on that occasion I cannot be presumed to know how far Mr. Peers' statement is correct; but when he proceeds to say that "knowing the Penketh report to be incom- plete, he suspects the integrity:of that of Wycliffe," I simply ask, wherefore? This is clearly too fast. The false start, however, has been made; and our friend steps out further with an "I am quite sure the absent critics got a very good mauling "—a process quite super- fluous since a special point of the paper lay in exhibiting, how the critics "maul "one another. But " the repor- ter must have omitted to tell"—so the reasoning proceeds —"who it was stood up for the poor downtrodden critics "—a hard matter for the poor reporter since no one did stand up for any such purpose. But to jump to a conclusion—since "fair play demands this,"says Mr. Peers " I infer it was so !" Charming logic ! Now I have no time to follow our friend through other remarks of his, quite irrelevant to my paper. I will only add that the above specimen of Mr. Peers' imperfect reasoning very aptly illustrated the larger por- tion of that modern "criticism" against which "common sense" recoils : .
Ist. There is a suspidon OA some meagre basis that all_is not as if. seems.

2. After much wrangling and a" very good mauling" , of one another the" critics "conclude that omissions here and interpolations there and forgeries everywhere must have taken place in the Scriptures. 3. Since the theory absolutely demands this, "We infer that it was so " ! Credat Judreus !—Yours, JOHN DIGNUM.
Penketh, 11th December, 1890,
NEWTON POLICE COURT AGAIN!

Sir,—The above Court seems determined ta get noto- riety at any price. A short time ago its name was bandied about the papers for granting a license in defiance of the voice of the people. That will not be forgotten in a hurry; especially will the memory of it be fresh when the ballot boxes are brought round. I hope when that time comes, those black tins will hold the death warrants of several absurd systems which are now in existence. rust and foremost is the licensing system. Reason was held at

bay when the Newton bench, in spiteof protest from thE inhabitants, laid a most important site at the disposal of a tumbledown public-house. It passes all comprehension to see why they are so anxious to keep up the number of public-houses. Are they like the doctor who said that, while he did not care to see everybody violently ill, he nevertheless liked to see folks a little bit sick in order that he might have something te. ela,? Are the magis- trates similarly afraid of having nothing to'do if they shut up the public-houses? Apart from the licensing question, there are many other drawbacks attached to the present unpaid magis- tracy. Then again, there is what Mr. Justice Wills calls "an abominable system." His lordship, with all the solemnity of wig and robes, pointed it out last Friday at the Liverpool Winter Assizes during the hearing of a case of house-breaking from Newton.. He observed that "the magistrates'-clerk at the Newton Pelice Court was also the prosecuting solicitor in the case. He had no idea lof suggesting that it would influence- a gentleman because he was going to have the charge of the prosecution, but still, he would ask, what would people think of him (the Judge's) position if he were to get a guinea for every ' person he convicted, and nothing for those who were not convicted? All the prestige and all the traditions which himg about the bench would be.shaken if a judge was to receive a pecuniary benefit from his decisions. A magis- trates' clerk was almost practically in the position of saying whether the prisoner should be committed or not, for he was consulted by the magistrates. He hoped to see the day when such an abominable system would be prohibited by Act of Parliament." We teetotallers are sometimes twitted for using strong adjectives, but we cannot exceed in severity the judge's remarks. However, we hope to seethe environment of the present courts of law completely changed, so that a II cases will be tried before a suitable tribunal, and the licensing question in particular wiTh be regulated in full accordance with the wishes of the people.— Yours truly, Dec. Bth, 1890.
PRO-STIPENDIARY.
"COUNCILLOR H. ROBERTS- AND A MEMBER OF THE. WATCH: COM MITTEE." THE CASE OF EX-P.S. SHAW.

Sir,—l am glad to notice that the result of my former letter has been to compel your correspondent to disavow the discreditable suggestion contained in his first letter, viz., that" Shaw "had been " shamming" during a por- tion of time when he was absent from duty. Now, as I am a little bit 6 behind the scenes," although not a mem- ber of the Watch Committee, I know for a positive fact. that " Shaw's " opponents on the Witch Committee and elsewhere; have repeatedly- made tha same insinuation, and do not hesitate to do so still, but not one of them dares to make the charge in a public; manner, because it would be capable of such easy refutation. The only reason why your correspondent now repudiates the charge is, because I showed in my last letter how, seriously persisted in, it would involve both the haneur and capacity of one or more medical men of undoubted integrity and ability. The " job " perpetrated by the Watch Committee, both in regard to the enforced retirement of "Shaw,?' and in the appointment of his successor, was a very dirty one all through, and is quite "of a piece" with the action of the caries men who vote against my election upon the Watch Committee, because I am a teetotaller, and in the same breath support the election thereon of a , wholesale and retail brewer and publican. Your correspondent is terribly upset because I accused him of cowardice, inasmuch as he had not &led to say in the Council Chamber, where he is open to eontradie- tion, what he has asserted in, his letters. His excuse that the proceedings of the Watch, Committee are not open to discussion in the Council is all, moonshire. The proceed- ings were discuised, and your correspondent took part in the discussion. Why is this Member ca the Watch , Committee" always so zealous in defence of the actions of the Chief Constable? What is the nature of their in- timacy ? Is it a case of a "quid pro quo?" The rest of your correspondent's effusion consis en- tirely of a gross personal attack upon myself, and there- fore, while' am aware that it will gra-ify such few - yourozild....ers as may, like the Co • ' •

iiriEleir natures have tqllFaa taste for the fetid literary garbage offered them by such a writer, I am 'well content to leave' My conduct to the discerithg judgement of an unbiassed and fair-minded arm trying to do my duty in the. Council, sometimes with only few to help me, and fre- quently with great odds against me, and, being t times Anl4,ble. to call a "spade" by arty other Mune, the' sen- sibilities of the "Miss Nancy's" of the Council are occasionally shocked thereby, and they tell ins I make "very improper remarks," but even that terrible censure does not appal me and as" Nil desperandumP, is my motto, I shall keep "pegging away" at all abuses that come under my notice.—l am, yours,
R. ROBERTS.
COUNT TOLSTOI AND CHRISTIANITY.-WHAT
IS A CHRISTIAN?

Sir,—Mr. Peers seems to be unable to understand how Tolstoi can be a Chriatian and yet reject the dogma of the Fall of Man. He says that the rejection of this dogma necessitates the rejection also of the Redemption. This is certainly quite true— and Tolstoi rejects both dogmas. But why, on that ground, ,Tolstoi should be a literary and logical phenomenon I fail to understand. At least it is notrhis Lult if he be such a phenomenOn. since he gives very sufficient reasons for such rejection. He distinctly says that Christ never once mentions these dogmas—that they have been foisted on Christianity without one word from Christ in support of them. And I should like to ask who we should zo to •for Christain dsctrines, if not to Christ himself.

And regarding the Redemption, or the Atonement, I believe there is not one word in the Gospels that in. any way touches on this dogma. The word Atonement, is I not once mentioned by Christ. On the contrary Christ was always telling men of the hive of the Father for ,His children—of His yearning 'eve and tenderness and pity for them. He nowhere teaches that, before the Father can be reconciled, a price must be. paid—blood must be shed. Nowhere cloes He teach that, the Father. I must be,propitiated before He can forgive His children. On the contrary, to show the fullness of the 'Father's love, He giVes us the beautiful and touching parable of , the prodigal son. When the poor prodigal awakened to a full sense of the utter debasement to which he Lad fallen and determined to turn his back upon it all and go home to his father, his father was on the look out for him and saw him whilst he was yet a long way off, and ran to meet him and fell on his neck and kissed him. ' And when the poor fellow began to cry out " Father I have sinned," the father didn't even listen to him, hut called out to his servants, " Bring the best robe and put it on him; put shoes on his feet and a ring on his hand, and kill the fatted calf, and let us be merry ; for this my son was dead and is alive again ; he was lost and is found." Not a word here about any Recoppence, or Propitiation, or Atonement,not even a suggestion of such a thing. Touching the dogmas of the Fall and the Redemption, Tolstoi argues that they are altogether untenable—that they are, in fact, absurd. He says that, according to orthodox belief, man was created happy, immortal and without sin, " The felicity of man consisted in the enjoyment of life without toil, his immortality was due to the promise that his life should last for ever; his in- nocence was due to the fact that he had no conception of evil." But man was tempted by the devil and he fell, " and from this time men have endured toil, sickness, suffering, death ; the physical and moral struggle for existence." He goes on to show that if men have en- dured these evils through Adam having fallen, then, if Christ, by His death, has atoned for the sin of Adam and for the sins of all men since Adam's time, man onght to be restored to his former state of happiness, and sin- lessness, and immortality. But such is not the case. The evils which afflicted humanity from the expulsion of Adam from paradise until the birth of Christ, have con- tinued to afflict humanity from the birth of Christ down to the present day under exactly the same conditions. " But this doctrine does not concern itself too closely with the practical result of the Redemption, in virtue of which, the earth, after Jesus' coming, ought to have become once more, at least for believers, everywhere fertile.without need of human toil. Sickness ought to have ceased, and mothers have borne children without pain." "Of the struggle between animal in- stincts and reason this doctrine takes no account. All the love for truth and goodness in the heart of man, all his efforts to illuminate his spiritual life by the light of reason, are not only of; slight importance, according to this doctrine ; they are a temptation, an incitement to pride. Life as it is upon this earth, with all its joys and all its splendours, its struggles of reason with darkness, —the life of all men who have lived before me, my own life, with its inner struggles and triumphs,—all this is not the true life ; •it is the fallen life, a life irretrievably bad. The true life, the life without sin, is only in faith, that is, in imagination, that is, in lunacy." He goes on to say that if anyone would break the habit contracted m fro infancy of believing all this, and would look boldly at it without prejudice, this doctrine would appear to such a man as the product of absolute insanity. And yet Tolstoi believes in the divinity of Christ. He believes that Ile is the Messiah, the Saviour of men. But he believes that it is the life of Christ—not his death— that is the Salvation of our race, for His life was a re- velation to us of what our lives may be—lives of godli- ness, of purity, of absolute self-sacrifice and devotion to others. He is truly a Christian, for he believes literally and unreservedly in the teachings of Christ. Do ortho- dox Christians so believe in them P He takes the Ser- mon on the Mount and gives passage after passage and argues, and I think proves, that Christ really meant what he said. I have never yet met with Christians who believe that He did. I have never yet met with any who believe that Christ really meant that we are not to resist evil, that, if a man strikes us on one cheek we are
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13. 1890.

o turn to him themther also. .Nor have I met with any rho believe that if a man steals their coat they ire to give him their cloak also. I have yet -,o learn that in Christian Churches it is really believed that it is blessed to be poor in spirit, or to be meek, f rue, these things are inculcated, but whoever dreams of cultivatingthem ? Ess) the preachers themselves? I at any rate, havenever observed that these are distin- guishing traits amongst them. Then, I ask, "What is a Christian ?" Is it one who,really believes and practices the teachings of Christ, or is it one who bcdfeves doc- trines that he never taught.. and who, whilst? extolling the teachings asset forth irutbe Sermon on the 'Mount, yet affects to believe that they are, in overydayr life, im- practicable, that, in fact,. Christ never really meant *hat be said ? Since Mr. Peers-has such a logical' mind; he will probably have no difficulty in answeringratis ques- tion.—Yours
JOHN GANDY.

THE CANAL. AT THELWALL..

Although it is about a month since the nveriburst into the Ship Canal cutting,. there has been 120 material change in the aspect of the Thelwall section, which still presents a scene of the wreck. The height of the water has not to any great extent Itssened, and its surface at the rear- of the hospital is covered with wreckage. Some additional pumping machinery has been placed near the locks, and this as welleas the old pumps are continually kept working. Near, the com- pany's offices at Morriebrook an embankment has been made across the cutting, and another is akilost com- pleted at Statham. The water between these-points will be allowed to remain in the cutting, which is practically finished for that distance. The steam navvy-which was buried by the flood has been taken to pieces wader water and brought to the surface, decidedly much worse for its I protracted immersion. As the water gradualty subsides the amountof damage alone by the flood becomes more and more apparent. Almost all the working liaeswill have to be reconstructed. Tbelwall section a few week ago, one of activity, now presents a comparatively desolate appearance. Very few men are engaged, and a large nnmber of the employes have gone elsewhere in search of work. The length of canal between Knertsford-road and Twenty-step Bridge was not affected by- the second flood, and it has now been pumped dry.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE ON THE CRISIS.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE ON THE CRISIS.

Mr. Gladstone journeyerlheine from tondon on Thum- day, and made a short staY,-first at Retford and after- wards at Worksop, in order to address the electors of the Bassetlaw division in furtherance of the candidature of Mr. Mellor. At Retford, speaking to a crowd of people assembled on the railway platform in response to an address, the right hon. gentleman confined his remarks to Ireland and the Parnell difficulty. Why, ho asked, should English politics, and Scotch and Welsh polities, be dependent upon the choice of an Irish leader? ftecent events. afforded an additional reason why we should set ourselves free from the burden that is imposed upon us by the management of entirely Irish concerns. He stated that, after the Divorce Court proceedings having waited in vain for some spontaneons action on the part of Mr. Parnell—he com- municated to that gentleman through Mr. M'Carthy his belief that the effect of his (Mr. Parnell's) continuance in the Irish leadership would be to wreck the cause ot Home Rule in this country. But Mr. Parnell was now no longer the leader of the Irish National party, though with a minority he wai endeavouring to insist on the leadership, which had been taken from him by the constitutional representatives of Irrland. Daring the last five years the work on which the Liberal party had been directly em- ployed in Parliament was that of resistence to coercion, and that work, whoever might be the leader of the Irish people, remained as sacred and as urgent as ever. Speaking at Worksop, the right hon. gentlemen said he was glad to find that the people of that district were of one mind with the people of Retford, and thought that they ought not to abandon the cause of Ireland be- cause of anything that had happened in connection with an individual. He could not, however, discharge his duty without endeavouring to make it known every- where that the determination of the Liberal party was final and irrevocable, and that they could not undertake the business of prosecuting effectually at the coming elec- don the cause of Home Rule in connection with a particu • lar name. Having thus briefly referred to the Irish cause, he proceeded to remind his audience of the legislative needs of this country. The business of this country, he said, had long been in arrear, and in arrear it must always continue until by means of Home Rule we get rid of the Irish question. Many important reforms had to be carried out in this country, and he hoped the people of Worksop would assist in the work by returning to Parlia- ment "a representative who would reinforce the Liberal ranks, continually growing by new accessions from every portion of the country, and by fresh displacements of those Tor' and Dissensient candidates who were re- turned irk 1886, under erroneus impressions, and in conse- quence of pledges all of which they have forfeited." Mr. Gladstone, re-entering his saloon carriage, left Work- sop amidst loud cheers. Mr. Gladstone arrived at Hawarden Castle shortly after live o'clock, journeying via Liverpool-road Station, Chester, in a special train to Hawarden.

Yesterdaylifternoon the annual prize to the students .at this college took place- The Right Rev., the Lord Bishop of, Shrewsbury presided, and there were also present, the Dean. of Manchester, (hon. sec. of the College)4 Archdeacon of Chester, the Revs. Canon Pbnrhyn, Canon Mason (Kirk- ham), JLIJScott (Ordsall, Salford),J.. Th. Evans, P. E. Hop'wood. /la P. Reline, Ji.Nexini.Si. Wilkinson, F. W. Willis, .Dr. G. Watkin,ths Principal (the Rev. Morley Stevenson), and manyfriends,, and relatives of the students.

The linincipal in his statement of the work done in the college, during the• year said that he. might divide the audience into three parts. First of all there were his students, secondly the relatices, and friends of the stucleats, and lastly they had certain friends who were kind enough to attend year by- year, many of whom, he was glad to say, had no connection with the college but who- were so, good as to presont• themselves to show their iaterest in their and interest in tho• work of the college ' ' ' • hat College, and he would like'tesay that the results were
Liege,

factery2 The result of- the examination in music was als6 encouragihg,.for Sir. 3.6hn Stainer-reported upon it that from a mnsieal point of. view theCollegeheld a high place, and that 27 students out of 42C carried oft the full marks ith ease. !the re3Ults of., the examination of •needlework, which vies examined by Mrs. Coburn, and . the results the science examination were very good indeed. ToThis mind, the- great want of the College at the present time was that it should be extended. They were outgrowing their bUilding altogether, and they, wanted to enlarge the College. They also wanted a pre- paratory class for those who wished to enter the College,' they wanted more accommodation for their teachers,and they WantedVredeation room. tor their present stu- dents. Tho Principaltxmcluded amidst applause. ' The Bishop of Shrewsbury said Warrington had always held a very. high place in England on account of it con- taining a training college. Having made reference to the late ream. of Warrington, whom, he said, had the largest share in the foundinp of that college, the Lord Bishop spoke ca free or assisted education, and concluded by urging the students to strivo on in whatever, spheres they might be called to, and always do their Utmost to impart a good, secular, and Divine knowledge. (Ap- plause).. The prizes and certificates were then distributed to the successful students, after which, , The Dean of Manchester proposed, and the Archbishop of Chester seconded a vote of thanks to the Bishop of Shrewsbury, and his Lordship having briefly responded, the meeting terminated.

div.head: HOUSEBREAKING AT NEWTON.
div.p: HOUSEBREAKING AT NEWTON.
TIIE JUDGE AND TIM NRIVTON 3IAGISTRATES' CLEItt.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Friday, Kate MeMU, a servant, aged seventeen years, was acquitted ' of the charge of breaking into the houie of Frederick Shallcross, at Newton, on September 19th,and steal- ing 19.5. 4d. Mr. 11. Swift prosecuted; and Mr. Segar was for the defence. During the hearing of the case, MT. Justice Wil.s, in whose court it was taken, elicited the fact that no information of the alleged Offence was given to the police until a week after it was said to be committed.—His lordship said he noticed that the magistrates' clerk at the Newton Police Court was also the proisecuting solicitor in the ease. Although he had no idea of suggesting that it would influence that gentleman because he was going to have the prosecution if the prisoner were going to be sent for trial, still he would ask what people would think of his (the judge's) position if he were to get a guinea for every person he convicted, and nothing for persons who were acquitted ? All the prestige and • all the tradi- tions which hung about the bench of justice would be shaken if a judge was to get pecuniary beriefit out of what he decided. A magistrates' clerk was almost practically in the position of saying whether a prisoner should be committed or not, for he was consulted by the magistrates. He hoped he would live to see the day when such a practice would be pro- hibited by an Act of Parliament. It was his duty to see that people where not convicted upon unsatisfactory evidence, and he had elicited a fact which he thought those presiding on the magisterial bench might have noticed—namely, the long delay before the charge was made.
Mr. Swift: I hope your lordship will allow,' me to say it is the custom in the county that this shall be done, and my instructor's firm is a highly respectable one.

His Lordship: I have not the slightest suspicion that these gentlemen's opinion would be warped by the facts. I think, however, that it is an abominable system, and so I am sure everyone would feel if a judge was to receive a sum according to the decisions he gave. These gentle- men are no doubt of the highest respectability, but I think they should help in an agitation 'should:like to set up to abolish the system. lam sorry for thenstand sorry to have to say a word about it. Mr. Swift: I am afraid my friend's business may suffer if he does as your lordship suggests. His Lordship: If it unfortunately did,i should have all the more respect for him.

The "Daily News" says :—Can a magistrates' clerk fitly undertake the duties of a prosecuting solicitor, ? Mr. Justice Wills declares that he cannot; and the reasons appear to be cogent and obvious. In the first place magistrates are in the habit of consulting their clerks as persons possessing, as a rule, both legal knowledge and practical experience, so that this official is really often in the position of saying whether a prisoner shall be committed or not. " What," asked the judgp. "would people think of me if I were to get a gc.inea for every person convicted, and nothlng for those who are acquitted ?" In the instance that gave rise to these remarks it appeared that there had been a. aelay ofra week in giving information to the police of an alleged case of housebreaking fund stealing on the pQrt of a ser- vant girl aged seventeen. M. Justice Wills was careful to guard against being supposed to throw "the slightest suspicion' upon the clerk of the Newton Police Court ; but he was not the less emphatic in denouncing the system as "an abominable one," which ought to be " prohibited by Act of rarlianaent."
